Small but mighty, the Poldina lamp suits functionality more than expressive design without making an eyesore of itself. The lamp is suitable for indoors or outdoors, and its slim stature allows it to slot into the tightest spacest—meaning more room on your bedside table for an attractive alarm clock, skincare, paperback, and other nighttime essentials. Shopping writer Julia Harrison has this rechargeable table lamp in a sage matte, and finds it to be perfect task lighting for a desk or a little mise en place work in the kitchen. “It blends shyly and seamlessly into all setups that require a little, but not too much, light,” she says.

This lamp is pricey, but think of it as functional art. In a perfectly dim room it emits the most ethereal glow.

Lee admits that most of her lighting inspiration comes from Quarters, the vibey design showroom and retail concept space by Felicia Hung and Nick Ozemba of In Common With. “Good fixtures are a given when your space is put together by lighting designers, and there’s no shortage of excellent lamps, sconces, and chandeliers at every corner,” says Lee. For her, In Common With’s Fazzo lamp shines a smidge brighter than the rest. Amber-hued glass looks as though it's been draped on the rounded head of a bulb, resulting in a wispy silhouette and a glowy presence even when switched off. “I’ve been fortunate enough to attend a number of functions at Quarters and I always leave with a little less storage on my phone but 100 new lamp photos,” says Lee.

Because of the opaque shade, this lamp casts a softer, more diffused light than clear or fabric shades.

Inspired by Italian modernism, the mushroom shape of Rejuvenation’s Roland table lamp is made entirely of glass. The petite frame is only 10 inches tall, and the lamp casts a soft glow, diffused by the opaque shade. Despite not being dimmable, this bestseller’s light is never hard or stark white. Use this lamp for ambiance in your living room or on your bedside table.

The geometric form is completely transparent, showcasing all of the internal wiring and the light bulb. McGregor says that it’s also a notably heavy fixture.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent drew inspiration from 1940s architecture for this hand-cast glass lamp, which you may recognize as an honoree from our 2025 Best in Show edit. Pewter accents and subtle texture bring a contemporary elegance to the organic materials, giving the fixture inherent Brutalist appeal that swayed shopping market editor Kate McGregor. “This piece casts the ideal warm glow across my entire work surface. Solid and weighty, it’s the kind of lamp that will blend seamlessly with my decor evolution, whether it leans more eclectic one day, and more mod the next,” she says. McGregor notes that the design’s transparency translates to a visible lightbulb “which, with my current standard bulb, I’m not sure how I feel about, but with an eddison or big globe option, it becomes a statement,” she says.

Interiors guru Shea McGee brings her penchant for reimagining classic design with this coastal table lamp. While its bulbous base draws your eye, the sloping shade gives it a more traditional silhouette. Wrapping the entire design in wicker brings a contemporary twist, reminiscent of our new favorite movie. This fixture is a versatile choice—we picture it accenting more reserved interiors or eclectic design schemes , especially in the ‘chive’ green hue.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

The Lulu & Georgia Camas Table Lamp is a masterclass in mixing materials. Grounded by a no-frills brass base, the dramatically ruched linen shade is the main force driving this lamp’s design. Ribbons on each side of the shade’s base layer in even more texture and charm, tying the piece together (pun intended).

Bulb type: A19 LED Filament Bulb, 9W recommended

Care for an infusion of rustic Italian farmhouse style? Heidi Caillier’s on the case. Decorative lug handles and a green glaze suggest heirloom. Your secret? There’s no Tuscan vineyard written into your inheritance, though this lamp might have your guests assuming otherwise.

Don’t sleep on IKEA’s newer collections. The spherical FADO lamp has taken over TikTok because of its versatility with a number of different interior design styles. Our favorite tip? Use a smart lightbulb to change the color (say, pink or orange) for a tasteful pop of whimsy in your home.

Anointed a reader favorite from our Best in Show lookback, this mixed material light from Istanbul-based designer Merve Kahraman embraces the checkerboard trend with a coastal edge. It’s available in two different sizes to accent bedside tables, credenzas, or consoles of all proportions, and supply a subtle amount of color in either green or red. It’s important to note that you need a particularly narrow bulb to fit in the rattan shade, as it doesn’t disassemble.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

We think traditionalists will gravitate towards this streamlined pick from AD100 firm Pierce & Ward. The design's flattened surfaces feel like a novel take on form, bringing just the right amount of dimension to your nightstands or desktops. The dandelion-hue linen shade offers just a hint of color, while the rounded ceramic base’s earthy finish feels like a natural fit in a minimalist’s space.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

“This delightful, kelly green lamp changes brightness levels with the touch of a button and charges in mere hours—it even goes outside,” muses McGregor. Rechargeable and portable, the Suki lamp from Kate Spade is minimal but bold, suiting a plethora of design styles from midcentury to space age and postmodern. “I’m a sucker for a portable lamp, and this one that actually has the power to illuminate my entire bedroom in an ambient glow,” says McGregor,

The best part of this Gantri table lamp is its 26 different color-blocking combos.“If I could, I’d have 12 of these lamps across my house, each with a different color base,” says shopping writer Julia Harrison. While her Lago sits atop a stack of books on her desk, it’s been known to move around her house to function as a reading light, a bedside table lamp, and task lighting for late-night puzzling. The Lagos sheds a warm white light perfect for winding down and doing a bit of reading (ie: scrolling) before lights out. The red base and white shade would look particularly cute bedside, especially next to a striped bedding setup.

While you can use a higher watt light bulb than your light fixture suggests, we wouldn’t recommend it. Wattage relates to how much power a particular device uses, and if more than the design allows is being used, you face the risk of ‘overlamping,’ meaning your fixture will start to run particularly hot. This is bad for a few reasons: Overheating can melt bulb sockets and wiring and, in the worst cases, lead to an electrical fire. It may also cost you more in the long run and be less energy-efficient—if your bulbs are drawing too much energy, it’ll likely mean having to replace them more frequently. If you’re still confused on the correct bulb to look for, we hope this handy visual guide will help.

And that’s saying something, as I battle-tested this quilt in a New York laundromat where it endured high heat and no option for a gentle cycle.

At $190 for a total bed refresh, this high-quality set is a nice buy. I love how it lies, and I believe it’ll be a big win for anyone who hates making their bed. It skews a bit casual for my maximal taste, but I love the warm ivory option for a great guest-room spread, where I keep things more uniform and less lavish. Ultimately, the weight, the feel, and the price point make it one of the most solid quilt-set choices I’ve come across in my very diligent searching.

#4970. Liquid Network Restores Full Bitcoin Backing Two Months After $320M Exploit

Liquid Network Restores Full Bitcoin Backing Two Months After $320M Exploit

The Liquid Network's Bitcoin reserves have been fully restored, two months after self-described white-hat hackers drained most of them, the Liquid Federation said on Monday.

The federation said it had reestablished 1:1 Bitcoin backing for all LBTC, the token that represents Bitcoin on Liquid. The milestone follows the restoration of swaps between BTC and LBTC at a 1:1 rate through participating providers several weeks ago, it said.

The Liquid Federation is pleased to announce that the network’s bitcoin reserves have been fully restored, reestablishing 1:1 BTC backing for all LBTC.

This follows the restoration of BTC<>LBTC swaps several weeks ago, which have since allowed…

— Liquid Network 🌊 (@Liquid_BTC) November 3, 2026

Blockstream CEO Adam Back, whose company develops the technology behind Liquid, posted a screenshot of the network's dashboard showing assets matching liabilities at 100%, with a reserve deficit of 0.00 BTC. Users running their own Liquid nodes can verify the federation's reserves directly, the federation said.

It did not say how the shortfall left by the hack was covered.

Launched by Blockstream in 2018, Liquid is a Bitcoin sidechain, a separate blockchain that runs alongside Bitcoin, designed for faster and more private transfers. Users lock up BTC in a wallet controlled by the federation, a group of exchanges and other crypto companies that run the network, and receive the same amount of LBTC in return.

Asked on X what would stop a repeat of the hack, Back listed three hardened "lines of defense": refreshed peg-out authorization keys now held in cold hardware wallets, disabled proof validation caches along with a bug fix for nodes, and consensus rules that have been hardened to "fail closed." The network has also been through multiple third-party audits, he said.

"And lesson: treat with suspicion (don't trust, verify) AI suggested fixes," Back wrote.

Back had pointed to AI's growing role in security in an interview with Bloomberg Television on October 20, describing "a wave of AI-assisted security analysis" over the previous couple of months. "AI, of course, is a tool to help develop code and to secure the code, but also it can be used to find defects," he said, adding that it had been "affecting many companies in the sector." He said then that the hacked funds remained "under investigation."

The federation said it is modernizing Liquid's governance structure, introducing clearer responsibilities and oversight, and adding further technical and operational safeguards, with more details to come in the coming weeks.

On September 6, purported white-hat hackers withdrew about 4,000 BTC, then worth around $320 million, from Liquid's federation wallet, communicating with Blockstream through PGP-signed messages embedded in Bitcoin transactions.

The next day, they returned 3,400 BTC, worth about $269 million, after Blockstream said Liquid's bridge nodes had been patched, but kept roughly 598 BTC. Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet said that if the remaining coins were a negotiated reward, the arrangement looked "more like extortion than white-hat hacking."

Blockstream later refused to pay a ransom for the outstanding Bitcoin. "Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure," the company said. "It is not white-hat activity. It is theft."

#4968. Binance’s net inflows turn positive at $2.3B as withdrawals expand

Binance led exchanges in 24-hour net inflows, reversing Monday’s heavy outflows as it restored access to funds after its $6.3 billion hack.

Binance recorded $2.3 billion in net inflows over the past 24 hours as it expanded withdrawals following last week’s $6.3 billion hack.

The exchange led centralized exchanges tracked by DefiLlama in 24-hour net inflows. Bitfinex recorded about $280 million and Bitget about $127 million over the same period.

“By 03:00 UTC, we are seeing hourly deposits exceed withdrawals, reflecting improving user activity and stabilizing flows,” Binance said Tuesday on X.

The inflows mark a reversal from Monday, when Binance recorded more than $7 billion in 24-hour net outflows. OKX led exchanges with about $445 million in net inflows at that time.

Binance suspended withdrawals on Friday after Thursday’s $6.3 billion hack while it investigated the breach and conducted security checks. It began restoring withdrawals at 06:00 UTC on Sunday and reopened withdrawals for some fiat currencies on Monday, as outflows started to slow down.

In a Sunday recovery update, Binance said it had replaced approximately 95% of the affected assets. The remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that took longer to acquire through market and over-the-counter purchases.

The exchange has pledged to cover the losses using company resources and protection funds without passing them on to customers.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the attack to North Korea on Saturday. North Korea denied responsibility Tuesday, with Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, dismissing the allegation as “absurd rhetoric.”

#4965. Binance Misses Monthly Luna Classic Burn for First Time Since 2023

Binance Misses Monthly Luna Classic Burn for First Time Since 2023

Centralized exchange Binance has burned Luna Classic tokens on the first of every month since 2023, when Do Kwon's Terra Luna empire came crumbling down. At the start of November, however, that burn has not occurred.

Luna Classic (LUNC) is the original native token for the Terra blockchain, which Terraform Labs founder Do Kwon forked and left behind in 2022 in a bid to rescue his collapsing project. Kwon was later convicted of fraud and sentenced to 15 years in prison for his role in Terra’s $40 billion implosion. Yet the decentralized network he left behind has kept running, propped up by a passionate community of supporters who have sunk time, effort and money into keeping it alive.

Binance started the burns after Terra Classic’s community voted to burn a portion of every on-chain LUNC transaction in late 2022, with the exchange pledging to burn half of the trading fees earned from the token. In practice, this has come in the form of a batch of burns happening at the start of every month since March 2023, but, according to StatsBin data, November's burn has yet to come in.

Some Luna Classic investors are concerned about Binance's lack of monthly burn, while others point to last week's record-breaking hack of the exchange as a reason behind the burn's delay.

"It is an important sign of support and a vital part of the overall burn campaign," Dawid Skinder, brand and user experience ecosystem contributor for Terra Classic, told Decrypt. "It might be that it is just an operational issue after the biggest hack ever. Hopefully that is the case, Terra Classic does not need another problem."

Binance was hacked for $6.3 billion on Friday, which the FBI has attributed to TraderTraitor—the North Korean group blamed for the Bybit hack. It has been labelled the biggest crypto hack in history, with estimated losses at four times the previous record of $1.5 billion from the Bybit heist.

The exchange has been reopening withdrawals on the platform in stages, with the latest taking place late on Monday for dozens of Ethereum and Solana tokens. Some investors have questioned whether the LUNC burn is a priority for the exchange as it attempts to recover from the hack.

— Tango and Cash (@ThisDud30190229) November 2, 2026

"Yes, the hack was a problem," prominent Luna Classic community member Pedro, better known as Vegas, told Decrypt. "At the moment, we are helping them to keep LUNC and LUNA safe."

He has long claimed to be in direct contact with Binance regarding LUNC issues, though this has yet to be verified. Vegas claims Binance is working on security maintenance after the hack and is moving LUNC to a more secure wallet before proceeding with the burn.

Binance did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

The exchange has paused its LUNC burns once before, withholding contributions at the end of 2022 after the Terra Classic community voted to re-mint burned tokens as a development fund. Binance halved its burn to 50% of trading fees and only resumed in March 2023, once the community had scrapped the re-mints.

Luna Classic has dropped 7.9% in value over the past week to $0.0000417, per Decrypt data, and is down 99.99% from its all-time high of $119.18. Investors believe the Binance burn being paused is just one of many issues the token faces.

Skinder told Decrypt that Luna Classic needs to fix its lack of products, improve its marketing, conduct a proper audit, and protect itself against quantum attacks. Skinder said he believes in a revival but claims that it is difficult with decentralized governance and "amateur validators."

So, why bother? Why not spend time on another chain?

"There are X number of chains in a better state than Terra Classic. None of them (except Bitcoin, probably) have that history and narrative (biggest crypto revival ever). None of them have 20+ stablecoins that are waiting to be re-pegged and restored," Skinder said. "Low chance of success, big upside if done. Great history to be part of."

#4964. 11 Christmas Centerpiece Ideas That Are Fa-la-la-la-bulous

A festive Christmas centerpiece is not just a decorative focal point, it also sets the scene for making memories around the table. Whether you dream up a candy cane–inspired color scheme with elegant white china and poinsettia-red floral arrangements, or you create a winter tablescape complete with snowflakes, snowmen, and flickering tea lights, a holiday table is the perfect opportunity to get creative and channel your yuletide style. And the good news is, a holiday centerpiece isn’t just for a dining table—kitchen islands, foyers, and coffee tables all lend themselves well to a festive display. To inspire you, we’ve gathered our favorite Christmas centerpiece ideas that include everything from a classic cranberry-red palette to a designer’s chic jewel-toned Christmas table.

If you’re going for understated elegance, take cues from this Christmas table. Layer together natural elements like foraged foliage, evergreen branches, pinecones, and antlers, then add height with candleholders. “The palette is deliberately restrained and a departure from traditional holiday decor to maintain elegance and elevate the materials,” says Rae McCalmont of PBF Homes. The Christmas decor leans into deep forest greens, warm walnut tones, soft ivory, and earthy neutrals. “Layered greenery spills organically across the table to keep the presentation soft and unfussy, metallic hints, a mix of etched and colored glassware, and eclectic dinnerware elevate the presentation, while softly glowing candlelight introduces warmth,” McCalmont says.

“When planning for my Christmas dining table centerpiece, I found these fabulous candlesticks in amber, peach, and gold to complement my dining room wall mural without screaming ‘red and green’ like the typical holiday colors,” says Maggie Griffin, founder and lead designer at Maggie Griffin Design. She arranged the collection of candlesticks with white tapers down the center of the table, while “touches of jewel tones in the glassware and table linens add to the festive vibe and layered tabletop,” Griffin shares.

Pack a punch with a large Christmas arrangement that adds a festive pop of color. When assembling a seasonal DIY centerpiece, consider the vessel as an integral part of the arrangement. Here, Griffin layered seasonal magnolia and bright red berries in deep coral and celadon jars that she keeps on the kitchen counter year-round. “It’s a nod to the holiday season without the more traditional color scheme,” she says. “I believe in enhancing your home for the holidays, not totally redecorating it,” Griffin adds.

“We wanted the holiday decor to feel like a natural extension of the room rather than introduce an entirely new Christmas palette,” says Lindsey Herod, owner and principal designer at Lindsey Herod Interiors. The designer believes a room’s color story is a great starting point for any holiday table centerpiece. “Here, the centerpiece and holiday greenery can be lush and romantic because they’re speaking the same language as the chintz, antiques, and existing palette; it feels festive, but still completely part of the house,” Herod explains.

“It can be fun to look beyond traditional holiday themes and embrace decor that evokes the sense of magic and wonder that the season is all about,” says interior designer Bethany Adams, founder of Bethany Adams Interiors. For this centerpiece inspired by her late grandmother’s favorite china pattern, Adams wanted to create a quiet woodland that the deer on the mantel might have just visited. “A soft bed of moss, mushrooms of various sizes, and elegant taper candles lead the eye toward the mantel and its exuberant display of greenery,” she says. The best part? “Without obvious holiday themes, this centerpiece works all the way through the New Year,” Adams says.

Add a festive touch to a holiday party table or kitchen island with a custom gingerbread house. “We designed the gingerbread house as a playful nod to the home’s architecture, complete with an illuminated interior that echoes its expansive front entry windows,” says Kristi Will, founder of Kristi Will Interior Design. To make it extra special, the gingerbread house was personalized with the family’s dogs at the front door to welcome guests. “Created as the centerpiece for their holiday party, it brought a sense of whimsy and personality to the heart of the home,” Will says.

Embrace Christmas nostalgia by turning a vintage tabletop tree into a charming holiday centerpiece. Interior designer Bambi A’Lynn Bratton, founder of Bambi A’Lynn Interior Design, has a white Christmas tree, so this vintage German tree was the ideal choice for her table. “I have collected antique German ornaments for years and needed a special place to display them, so when I came across this little tree I knew it was the perfect fit,” she says. “I have also used this piece on a coffee table when I have a dinner party during the holidays, or on the hearth of a fireplace on top of a stack of books,” the designer shares.

For an elegant holiday table, you can’t go wrong with floral arrangements in classic Christmas red. “When it comes to styling the floral arrangements, I always make sure the florals are low enough so everyone at the table can see each other easily, but still bountiful enough so everyone can admire the gorgeous flowers used,” says interior stylist Carolyne Steiner of The Carolyne Collective. To complete the holiday tablescape, Steiner dotted white candlesticks in between the florals and placed ornaments on the plates. “I collect ornaments throughout the year for each guest invited to my event—it serves as their place card,” she shares. “Before we sit down for our meal, each person has to guess which place setting is theirs; it ends up becoming a really fun game, conversation piece, and icebreaker before dinner begins,” Steiner says.

Use a potted white orchid as an elegant Christmas centerpiece on a foyer table for a festive welcome. “The white orchid is just a lovely neutral decor item that adds some formality to a space,” says Grace Brackman, founder and principal designer at Grace Brackman Design. She notes that white orchids look particularly beautiful paired with more traditional decor. “Add some interest by potting it in a pretty ceramic bowl enhanced with some fresh-cut magnolia and fir,” Brackman suggests.

When creating a Christmas centerpiece, think beyond the surface of the dining table. “Decorating the chandelier draws the eye upward and makes the entire table feel more festive, rather than limiting the holiday elements to the tablescape itself,” says Lauren Sullivan, founder and curator at Well x Design. Here, red ribbon on the chandelier echoes the ribbon on the Christmas wreaths that hang from each chair, and visually extends the centerpiece beyond the table. “It also helps connect the table to the rest of the room and makes the whole setting feel more complete,” Sullivan says.

Arrange mercury glass trees and votive holders down the center of the dinner table to add height and create a magical ambience. “The reflective qualities of mercury glass make it a great choice for a candlelight dinner—it sets the mood and makes it feel extra festive,” Brackman says. To create an organic table runner and a soft backdrop of color for the trees to sit on, the designer recommends piling fresh-cut greenery at the base of the mercury pieces. “In my opinion, live greenery is a necessity as nothing beats the smell of fresh-cut pine,” Brackman states.

Morning Minute: Tom Lee Calls the Binance Hack Bullish for Ethereum

🐂 Tom Lee Calls the Binance Hack Bullish for Ethereum

Tom Lee looked at the largest crypto theft ever recorded and called the market’s response “constructive”. His company, BitMine Immersion, bought another 8,573 ETH last week, roughly $19.6 million worth, lifting the treasury to 6,060,506 ETH and about $13.7 billion. That’s 4.9% of the total circulating ETH supply, which makes Lee the most ETH-exposed executive on the planet.

His case comes down to one comparison. ETH fell about 4% after the $6.3 billion Binance hack. After the Bybit hack in February 2025, it dropped 8% on day one and 20% over the following week. Lee called that “relatively muted crypto market reaction very constructive” and read it as proof the industry can take a hit this size without cracking.

He pointed to four things behind the bullishness:

Each of those is a thing that went right in 2026 and went badly in 2025.

The price read holds up, but there are bigger questions for ETH’s future from a trading perspective. October was the worst month in the history of U.S. spot ETH ETFs, with $1.61 billion in net outflows. ETH is down 19% from its local peak, opposed to 11& for Bitcoin.

A potential driver of ETH’s weakness is Tom Lee himself. BitMine is now 99% of the way to the 5% supply cap Lee has said the company will stop at, about 49,500 ETH short, roughly six weeks at last week’s pace. #4961. NEAR token sinks 7% as proposal to cut annual token issuance passes

The proposed issuance cut would prevent 11.8 million NEAR from entering circulation over two years, worth about $45 million at today’s price.

Near Protocol’s NEAR token fell by roughly 7% on Tuesday, despite community approval of a proposal to gradually reduce the maximum annual issuance rate from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months.

NEAR traded at $3.82 as of 11:06 am UTC, extending its weekly decline to roughly 13%, according to CoinMarketCap.

The latest drop followed Monday’s approval of HSP-029, which received support from 99.9% of participating voting power. About 3.28 million vote-escrowed NEAR (veNEAR) tokens were cast in favor, according to the NEAR House of Stake governance platform.

The proposal would reduce long-term token dilution while lowering projected gross staking yields from 5.2% to 3.3% by the end of the 24-month period. It estimates that issuance would fall by 11.8 million NEAR over two years and 66.1 million NEAR over six years.

The proposal remains subject to the Security Council’s 14-day veto window. If not vetoed, it will be ratified, followed by a 90-day grace period before the issuance reduction begins. Implementation also requires validators to adopt the necessary technical upgrade.

#4959. 10 Must-Read Marvel Comics for VisionQuest Fans

As Vision’s MCU story gets stranger and stranger, these comics can help you understand his background—and give you a few more great stories to sink your teeth into.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FEW HEROES IN the Marvel Cinematic Universe have had it as rough as Vision. Since his debut in 2015’s Avengers: Age of Ultron, the Vision was mistrusted by the Avengers and forced to kill his creator, the homicidal robot Ultron. He fell in love with teammate Wanda Maximoff, only to fight against her in Captain America: Civil War, and then get killed by Thanos. A grief-stricken Wanda resurrected Vision in WandaVision and made him a father, using her hex powers to create twin sons. But when Wanda had to surrender her hex at the end of the series, he lost those children and was wiped from existence—but not before he transferred his memories into a white doppelgänger created by the government agency SWORD.

So where does that leave Vision? Very, very confused.

VisionQuest picks up with the White Vision from WandaVision, once again played by Paul Bettany. As he tries to make sense of the memories in his mind, memories that aren’t quite his, Vision seeks help from a collection of AIs from around the Marvel Universe, including personal assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Olra Brady) and thrill-seeker E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire). When a mysterious stranger sets a bounty hunter called the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to hunt him down, the Vision must call upon his worst enemy, Ultron (James Spader). Together, Vision and Ultron go on a journey that somehow reunites him with one of his sons, Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica), and takes him to the very beginning of artificial intelligence in the MCU.

But if you want your quest to go beyond the MCU, then check out these great Marvel Comics about Vision and his strange synthetic friends.

It all starts here, with Ultron’s first appearance in Avengers #55, his initial battle against Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, and his attempt to mimic his creator by making his own robot, a robot we know as the Vision. To MCU fans, the origin of Ultron and Vision broadly matches the plot beats of Avengers: Age of Ultron. But the specifics are different in the comics, where Ultron is the creation of Hank Pym aka Ant-Man, and the Vision is based on Wonder Man and the original Human Torch (more on that last guy in a minute).

Those differences alone would make “Behold… The Vision!” worthy reading material. But these issues stand on their own merit, classics of the Silver Age with delightfully wordy scripts by Roy Thomas and dramatic pencils by John Buscema. From these early beginnings, its easy to see how Ultron and Vision became Marvel mainstays.

If you’re going to read comics related to a show called VisionQuest, you should probably read the comic book storyline called VisionQuest, right? Yes! And, well… sort of. Written and drawn by the great John Byrne, VisionQuest is probably the height of West Coast Avengers, the series that focused on a California-based team of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, including Iron Man, USAgent, and Hawkeye. The story of the Scarlet Witch Wanda Maximoff’s search for her missing husband Vision, one that leads her to an all-white government copy and to the terrible truth about her twin children, Billy and Tommy, VisionQuest is a cracking superhero yarn.

But, as you might guess from the above synopsis, VisionQuest already appeared in the MCU, as one of the chief inspirations for WandaVision. As a result, VisionQuest TV series showrunner Terry Matalas had to take Bettany’s character in a new direction, one that involves Ultron and AIs more than it does Wanda or any of the West Coast Avengers. Still, Matalas draws from the foundation that Byrne laid in the comics, making VisionQuest a great read, no matter what else the MCU may have done.

Perhaps the most surprising thing about the adaptation of VisionQuest in WandaVision is that Marvel Comics actually published a series about Vision trying to have a happy sitcom life in the suburbs, and the show basically ignored it. The VisionQuest show doesn’t do much with that series either, but that doesn’t mean MCU fans should ignore it. In fact, the 2015 Vision miniseries remains not just the best Vision story ever written, but also one of the best comic book series of the 2010s.

Written by Tom King, who also wrote the excellent Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow and co-created the HBO show Lanterns, and illustrated by Gabriel Hernandez Walta and Michael Walsh, Vision finds the titular synthetic seeking normalcy. He moves to the the suburbs of Washington, DC, and creates his own family, complete with a wife, two kids, and a dog. But suburbia is never normal, with or without superheroes involved, and things get stranger by the second, forcing Vision to face some truths he’s spent his life avoiding.

One of VisionQuest’s central hooks is the chance to see the personalities behind some of the AIs who have been running the machines of the MCU. In addition to the aforementioned F.R.I.D.A.Y. and E.D.I.T.H., the show introduces us to personified versions of D.U.M.-E. and U (Henry Lewis and Jonathan Sayer), the robotic arms Tony Stark used in Iron Man, as well as Stark’s first AI J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy, somewhat reprising his role from Agent Carter).

Although many of those specific programs don’t appear in Marvel Comics, that world does have plenty of AIs, many of whom gathered with the Vision for the series Avengers AI. Set after the Age of Ultron event (more on that shortly), Avengers AI sees Vision and Ultron’s creator Hank Pym forming a team of robots to defend cyberspace, a team that eventually involves Jocasta—a robot bride Ultron built for himself, and who is a major part of the VisionQuest show.

In addition to Jocasta, VisionQuest could also bring in the Human Torch, the very first Marvel hero, thanks to his history with Vision. Introduced in 1939’s Marvel Comics #1, the Human Torch was an android invented by scientist Phineas Horton, an android who burst into flames when exposed to oxygen. While that Torch’s greatest legacy may be inspiring Johnny Storm of the Fantastic Four’s codename, his body became the basis for Vision, forever bonding the two heroes.

So great is that bond that the connection was repeated in the recent series The Ultimates. Set in an alternate reality ruled by the Maker, an evil version of Reed Richards of the Fantastic Four, the Ultimates are a rag-tag group of Avengers fighting to fix the word. The Ultimates think they lost an ally when Captain America’s World War II colleague goes missing. But they regain him again in a greater form as the Vision, a hero who controls the entire internet.

We’re going to be honest with you: the best Ultron story of all time is Ultron Unlimited, from Kurt Busiek and George Perez’s legendary Avengers run in the late ‘90s. Yet, for some reason, Marvel has decided to keep that series out of print, making it difficult to find outside of the Marvel Unlimited app… which will shut down by the end of the year.

Still, that doesn’t mean there are no good Ultron stories out there for hard copy collectors. Case in point, the first arc from 2007’s The Mighty Avengers, “The Ultron Initiative.” Written by Brian Michael Bendis and illustrated by Frank Cho, The Mighty Avengers promised big, classical superhero action in the aftermath of the Marvel Civil War. The Ultron Initiative delivered by putting Iron Man’s new team against a major threat and taking the story to ridiculous levels.

As much as Brian Michael Bendis nailed the character in The Ultron Initiative, his second take on Ultron went wildly, but entertainingly, wrong. Like the Avengers movie that shares its subtitle, Age of Ultron does indeed see Ultron try to reshape the world in an image he sees fit. But the similarities end there, and not just because Spader plays a more comedic and philosophical villain in the movies.

The story begins with Ultron having already conquered the world, covering the planet with his drones. As the Avengers lead a resistance, they discover that he’s already taken control of their teammate, the Vision, who promptly kills some of his friends. From there, Age of Ultron becomes a big mess of time travel and alternate realities, all built around the idea that Ultron is unstoppable. At the time of its release, Bendis intended the series to fix some messes in Marvel continuity, not unlike DC’s Crisis on Infinite Earth. In practice, the series raised more questions than it answered, making it something best enjoyed as a big ol’ sloppy mess.

Believe it or not, the breakout character of VisionQuest is neither the titular Avenger, nor any of the delightful AIs who help him. Rather, it’s the Paladin, a cold-hearted mercenary played by Todd Stashwick. With the help of his handler (Diane Morgan, aka Philomena Cunk), Paladin takes on a mission to capture the Vision, a decision that will forever change his life.

Anyone intrigued by Stashwick’s take would do well to check out Paladin’s comic book appearances, which start with 1977’s Daredevil #150, by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino. Like all pre-Frank Miller Daredevil comics, the story is cheesier than a modern reader would expect. But it does lay out a compelling costumed mercenary, one who becomes a fun weirdo over the next few decades of the Marvel Universe.

Wanda and Vision’s twin sons, Tommy and Billy, are not real. They came from Wanda’s magic and, as shown in WandaVision, they disappeared when she released her hex. Moreover, Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness showed us that Wanda turned villainous when she tried to find Tommy and Billy somewhere else, in another part of the multiverse. So that when Billy (Joe Locke) turned up alive as a magic-casting teen in Agatha All Along, he carried the shame of being a child of the Scarlet Witch.

VisionQuest brings back Billy’s brother Tommy, who eventually becomes the Quicksilver-esque Speed. We don’t know yet what Billy and Tommy will get up to together, but we can’t help but hope they’ll follow some of the beats from the Avengers and Young Avengers crossover, The Children’s Crusade. Written by Allan Heinberg and illustrated by Jim Cheung, The Children’s Crusade follows Billy and Tommy, aka Wiccan and Speed, as they try to rescue their mother Wanda, who has been taken by Doctor Doom. In doing so, they and their fellow Young Avengers clash against the adult Avengers, all to redeem the Scarlet Witch.

Whatever happens in the MCU, Wanda and Vision have not only been reunited in the comics, but their family has grown. Vision still has Viv Vision, the synthetic daughter he created in the Tom King series Vision, but Billy has married his longtime teammate Teddy aka Hulkling. Further, Teddy has become the head of the combined Kree and Skrull empires, making Billy royalty by law.

All of that is a long way of saying that when Ultron threatens the galaxy, no family is better qualified than Vision and co. to deal with it. That’s just one of the stories in the one-shot Raid of Ultron, which features tales written by Wyatt Kennedy, Tegan Quin, Josh Trujillo, and Zoe Tunnell, and the artwork of Stephen Byrne, Bradley Clayton, Rachael Stott, and Luciano Vecchio. But even when the stories in Raid of Ultron don’t deal directly with Vision, his presence is felt, proving that he’s become much more than a crazed robot’s science experiment.

#4953. Moscow Exchange to launch Bitcoin, Ether and USDT trading in December

Moscow Exchange plans to launch crypto trading on Dec. 1 under Russia’s new law, with annual purchase limits for non-qualified investors.

Moscow Exchange plans to launch trading in Bitcoin, Ether and Tether’s USDT on Dec. 1, opening what it describes as Russia’s first organized digital currency market.

The exchange said Monday that pilot trades would begin as participants join the platform. Trades will use its existing stock-market infrastructure and be cleared through the National Clearing Center (NCC), with trading hours from 6:50 am to 11:50 pm Moscow time.

The venue will initially support same-day and next-day settlement, as well as swap transactions. Non-qualified investors must pass a test before purchasing crypto and will be limited to purchases of 300,000 rubles (about $3,700) annually per broker, according to the exchange.

The launch follows a Russian crypto law whose main provisions took effect Sept. 1. The law permits regulated trading but maintains a ban on cryptocurrency payments for goods and services in Russia.

Moscow Exchange and the NCC have been under US sanctions since June 2024, when the UK also sanctioned the exchange. The European Union added it to its sanctions list in July 2026.

Sergey Mendeleev, founder of Russian cross-border payments platform Exved, told Cointelegraph he doubted the proposed market would attract significant demand.

“Neither the global nor the local market will notice anything at all,” he said, questioning who would trade on a sanctioned exchange.

Mendeleev also predicted uncompetitive trading conditions, comparing the prospective offering to precious metals accounts at Russian lender Sberbank, where customers trade account balances without taking possession of physical metal.

Related: Russia to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trades starting July 2027

He warned that investors could face “absolutely outrageous spreads,” referring to the difference between buying and selling prices. “For ordinary non-qualified investors, this is an entirely unattractive and unprofitable proposition,” he said.

Mendeleev saw potential for the platform to support cross-border payments. He said a venue where importers and exporters could buy and sell crypto directly with one another would be welcome, but questioned whether adding another intermediary would be competitive in a market where traders negotiate over price differences as small as 0.05%.

“I hope this will mark a genuine breakthrough for foreign trade,” he said.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

THREE REAL GUYS. Three dramatically different mental health conditions. Here’s how a weed card works for them.

THE GUY: TJ, a 47-year-old data insights professional

THE CONDITION: Multiple sclerosis, a chronic autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system

THE EXPERIENCE: TJ was diagnosed with MS at the age of 25. Doctors prescribed him Rebif, a drug that helped his symptoms but made him depressed. “I was immediately suicidal on that medicine,” he says. Years before medical marijuana was legalized in his state, a friend suggested pot. TJ was desperate, tried weed, and says he felt immediate relief. In 2022, he obtained his medical card. Today, TJ struggles with nerve pain and migraines but says cannabis helps him play volleyball, travel, and stay active. “I don’t know that I would have a productive and happy life if I were not treating myself that way.”

THE GUY: CJ, a 32-year-old postdoctoral researcher of addiction neurobiology

THE CONDITION: Sarcoidosis, an inflammatory disease that causes collections of immune cells, called granulomas, to form in the body. Depending on the location, granulomas can result in fatigue, joint pain, nausea, and swelling. CJ has a rare form located in his brain stem.

THE EXPERIENCE: CJ’s symptoms began in his early 20s, starting with skin issues and leading, eventually, to debilitating nausea. After doctors diagnosed him with sarcoidosis in 2021, he went from using cannabis occasionally to using it daily for nausea control. Through self-experimentation, he learned the combination of cannabinoids that worked the best. Because the ratios were harder to find in OTC products, CJ got his medical card in 2023. “This brought down my overall symptom load a huge amount,” CJ says. Along with an off-label Crohn’s disease medication, medical marijuana has brought him back to 90 percent of his old self, he says.

THE GUY: Jonah, a 41-year-old bookstore manager

THE CONDITION: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), a mental health condition that causes excessive fear and worry and interferes with day-to-day functioning.

THE EXPERIENCE: Jonah says he was always labeled “the weird kid.” He ran away at 16 and experienced problems with drugs, alcohol, and homelessness in his early 20s, until his mother convinced him to talk to a therapist, who diagnosed him with anxiety and recommended medical marijuana. After using cannabis for a few weeks, Jonah says, the dark fog that had made him want to act out or isolate himself began to lift. “Conversations with people became a lot easier; decision-making, especially good decisions, became a lot easier.” Sixteen years after that therapy appointment, he’s happily married and life is good, he says.

#4949. People Think They Drive Better High. These Scientists Are Testing the Theory.

Inside the lab that’s decoding the dangers of driving stoned.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

A HIT OR two from a friend’s vape at a party, a low-dose gummy at a concert, a THC-infused drink at a comedy show—the average guy would be fine to drive home a few hours after doing any of this, right?

Michael Stevens, PhD, director of the Clinical Neuroscience & Development Laboratory at the Olin Neuropsychiatry Research Center, has spent roughly a decade trying to answer that question. When I asked Stevens how long he’d recommend a friend wait before getting into a car after taking THC, he joked, “How much do I like this particular hypothetical friend?” before settling on three to six hours. Yes, that’s a huge range.

That uncertainty is a big issue right now, especially as cannabis legalization spreads across the U.S., and researchers beyond Stevens are raising concerns. One 2021 analysis found a 15 percent increase in fatal car crashes following marijuana legalization, and a separate review linked legalization to increases in car accidents, injuries, or fatalities.

Recently, Stevens and his colleagues conducted a lab study involving a high-tech driving simulator. The “car” looks something like an elite gaming rig, complete with a steering wheel, pedals, and a screen that features virtual roadways.

After tracking 19 performance metrics over several hours and examining brain activity through an MRI, researchers found that six of those metrics (roughly one-third) showed significant impairment following cannabis use. Stevens and his team witnessed drivers passing cars too closely or tailgating, increasing the risk of collision. Some drivers failed to make the necessary steering microadjustments to keep their vehicle centered in its lane.

It’s probably obvious that participants who inhaled higher-potency cannabis tended to drive worse than those who received lower doses of THC. But also, THC levels weren’t a strong predictor of who drove more dangerously—and when. Some participants’ dangerous driving faded gradually, says Stevens, while others’ worsened before improving. “The other thing that jumps out is that about two-thirds of people said they’d be willing to drive, even while admitting they still felt high and after we measured they were objectively driving worse,” Stevens says.

It’s true, 35 percent of people believe they drive better when high, according to a recent AAA survey. There is some truth there, says Stevens: People can be more cautious when they’re stoned. “But at the same time, being high whacks out many cognitive abilities,” he says. In Stevens’s study, people who drove while high tended to drive a little too slow, which can disrupt the flow of traffic, encourage other drivers to make risky passing maneuvers, and cause rear-end collisions.

Given what we know (and don’t) about how cannabis works in the body, it’s unlikely that we’ll find a magic THC number that tells us who is and isn’t impaired, at least in the near future. For now, Stevens says, the safest approach to cannabis and driving is pretty simple: When in doubt, wait it out. Regardless of how high you think you are—or aren’t—just call an Uber, text a buddy, or stay put.

ALL 50 HAVE an impaired-driving law that can apply to cannabis. But determining if a person’s too high to drive is all over the place.

Some states (Illinois, Montana, Nevada, Ohio, Washington) have been trying to apply the blood-alcohol framework to gauge drunkenness to cannabis by adopting a legal threshold, ranging between 2 and 5 ng/mL THC in the blood. These roadside assessments take time and aren’t lock-tight, because THC levels can plummet within 30 to 40 minutes of use. Many states (including California, Massachusetts, New York) use an effects-based approach, which looks for signs of impairment: erratic braking, slowed responses, bloodshot eyes. But that’s subjective. “You need a cut-and-dried kind of a test where there’s little room for error,” says Michael Stevens, PhD, of the Olin Neuropsychiatry Research Center. “Think of it like a mammogram screening—you really want the right answer.” For years, tech firms have been racing to develop a reliable roadside cannabis Breathalyzer. None have solved the core problem: Measuring THC isn’t the same thing as measuring impairment. That’s because THC sticks around in body fat. So if someone uses THC frequently, they have a reserve of the main psychoactive chemical that would throw off the test.

Rebecca is an alumna of Emerson College and The Boston Conservatory at Berklee, and her music can sometimes be heard on Boston radio stations, including 92.5 The River and Country 102.5. When she's not reporting or on the mic, she's usually chasing after her mischievous toddler, trying desperately to keep just one houseplant alive, or tinkering with her espresso machine in pursuit of the perfect iced honey latte.

#4946. ‘Scromiting’ and Other Super Scary Symptoms of Taking High-THC Weed

Yes, that’s vomiting and screaming at the same time.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

HIGH-CONCENTRATION SYNTHETIC THC products are producing wild reactions in some people. Kevin Gray, MD, a practicing physician and director of addiction sciences at Medical University of South Carolina, helps break them down.

“You experience hallucinations, paranoia, delusions,” says Dr. Gray. “It’s become undeniable looking at the association between teen cannabis use and psychosis that if somebody has some kind of already innate risk for developing a psychotic disorder, there’s something about use of cannabis during this stage of development that [may trigger the onset of] a lifelong disorder.” (The risk of someone developing the condition is less than 1 percent.)

“Paranoia is a symptom of psychosis. Instead of feeling the usual sort of high and calming feeling with cannabis, people feel more detached and more suspicious. Sometimes there will be a very high concentration or some unusual strain that may be more likely to lead to paranoia. The effect can be intense, but it’s transient and wears off with time.”

That’s screaming and vomiting at the same time. “Cyclic vomiting, cannabis-related emesis—I don’t see it that often among my clients, but it happens,” says Dr. Gray. “THC can reduce nausea, but there’s something about the interaction between THC and the systems that control our nausea that goes haywire in some people. We don’t know even how to treat it symptomatically, other than taking showers.” So if you totally misread a gummy label, just call 911—no judgment.

#4944. 30 Years of Legal Weed: Has It Made Us Any Healthier?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The very highs and bizarre lows of America on medicinal marijuana.

EARLIER THIS YEAR, during a brief and mercifully abandoned period when I was considering doing stand-up as a hobby, I went to a comedy show in downtown Austin. I was legitimately shocked to find, as part of the two-drink minimum bill of fare, the option for several different flavors of $5 THC seltzers. This wasn’t “take a pull off your vape or smoke a roach in the alley before the show” territory. No, marijuana drinks were on the menu.

In the past few years, my only social activities have been poker, competitive trivia, and going to the movies, all activities people do stoned, but not activities where you can literally order drugs from the bar alongside your chicken wings. The comedy club, on the other hand, considered marijuana products as a profit center.

This was one of those lightly attended weeknight shows where the comedians banter with the audience because they haven’t prepared much material. So, during a Q&A, I brought up the fact that there were THC sodas available to order, in laminate. “Sir, this is 2026,” the host said.

This is where we are now, a full three decades after California legalized medical weed. But is that good for us?

As I write this, it’s been eight-and-a-half years since I quit marijuana, a drug that at one point made pretty much anything—listening to music, shopping for groceries, cleaning the house—fun for me.

But really, I’ve been sober since I stopped using THC, since I was hardly just smoking there at the end. I was vaping, eating, drinking, dabbing, and otherwise gorging myself on what has become an extremely potent, psychosis-inducing drug. And I wasn’t having fun.

My breaking point, which I recounted in my 2020 memoir Pothead, came at Game 2 of the 2017 World Series at Dodger Stadium, where I was so wasted on weed that I had a screaming meltdown in front of security when I found out the ticket I’d bought was fraudulent.

It was a low point, a bottom so deep and so pathetic that I should have quit right there. But I went on for another three weeks before I finally crawled to a Marijuana Anonymous meeting and asked for help.

Now, nearly a decade later, I’ve emerged from my cocoon to find that THC is everywhere. I live in a state where it’s still technically illegal, but you can find some sort of THC variant in most convenience stores and in most bars and nightclubs.

My friend is an attorney who represents the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. He says his client is in a near panic. Sales are down for every beverage except for nonalcoholic mixers and those THC seltzers. THC is the beer, wine, and vodka of the present day, combined.

And so we find ourselves in a bizarre situation where people are drinking way less alcohol because it’s unhealthy for you, but they are instead ingesting THC products—either through soda, gummies, or any number of other concoctions—from unknown manufacturers, with unknown formulas and malleable dosages.

They’re also vaping, which emerging research is showing is kind of awful for our lungs. A University of Michigan study recently showed that teens who vaped cannabis were twice as likely to experience respiratory symptoms like “wheezing or whistling” in the chest than those who vaped nicotine or smoked traditional cigarettes.

Unlike traditional marijuana, this stuff isn’t “from the earth.” Who knows where it’s really from—or where it’s going?

When I quit weed in 2017, and somewhat loudly and publicly announced myself as an addict, I got the requisite amount of sympathy, but also a tremendous amount of pushback. Marijuana isn’t dangerous, people said. It isn’t addictive. It’s actually good for you.

In 2016, Gavin Newsom, then California’s lieutenant governor, spearheaded the legalization push for recreational marijuana. Cannabis sales have produced more than $8 billion in tax revenue for California since retail sales began in 2018, with a decent proportion of that funneled into teen substance-abuse prevention programs. But the state has also seen an increase in children suffering from cannabis poisoning.

It’s been a massive shift, moving from medically administered weed for veterans and cancer patients to powerful THC beverages you can buy at your bodega.

Legalization has created a new frontier of intoxicants without a centralized warning system for users. Data from a 2025 national study of U.S. adults stated that 15 percent of respondents reported daily or near-daily cannabis use.

Among those daily users, 18 percent reported experiencing symptoms consistent with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, a disorder characterized by cyclic, severe nausea, intractable vomiting, and gut pain alleviated temporarily by hot baths or showers.

This translates to an estimated 7.2 million people in the United States alone, many of them teenagers, experiencing these symptoms. That number is probably vastly underestimated, given that fewer than 12 percent of sufferers have received a formal diagnosis.

Welcome to the darker side of legalized weed, a world of cannabis-induced psychosis, “scromiting” (yes, screaming while vomiting), and concoctions like “shatter” or “wax,” which contain up to 90 percent THC, as opposed to the 3 to 5 percent in joints from previous decades.

So I find myself in a somewhat odd situation. I was a relatively early victim of modern weed’s potency, as well as a relatively early unadopter, and a very early voice in the wilderness warning the world that marijuana might not be the answer to all our health concerns. But now I find myself, like a patient waking up from a long coma, in a world where THC is as prevalent as, and cheaper than, whiskey. Yet still, I find myself thinking it should be legal. So which is it? Maybe we still don’t have enough data.

Thirty years since the start of legalization might feel like a long time, but it’s really not. In terms of scientific analysis, we’re still in relatively undiscovered country. If you’re suffering from chronic pain, or dying of cancer, marijuana is a healthier option than, say, oxycodone. But for the rest of us? No one really knows.

The only thing I can be truly sure of is that it’s no longer for me.

#4941. Weed Addiction Is a Real Thing. The World's Leading Cannabis Researcher Explains Why.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

KEVIN HILL, MD, the guy when it comes to this stuff. He’s the chief of the Division of Addiction Psychiatry at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. We talked to him about all the questions you probably have about weed and addiction.

Dr. Hill: Absolutely. Most people who use cannabis don’t develop a cannabis use disorder or cannabis addiction. But there has always been a subset of individuals who do. Five years ago, the data indicated about 10 to 30 percent of adults develop a cannabis use disorder. Now the published data says 30 to 35 percent. With the rise in potency, we’re seeing a rise in the number of users who are developing problems.

MH: Does cannabis use disorder differ from other addictions?

Dr. Hill: It affects a lot of the same neurotransmitters that other substances of abuse might affect. If you use cannabis, you’re going to have a surge in dopamine. Similarly, if you use opioids, you’re going to have a surge in dopamine, but the scale of it is different. It’s why a lot of medications we use to treat addictions operate on common pathways.

MH: Is there a genetic risk of developing a weed addiction?

Dr. Hill: Yes. The genetic aspects of cannabis use disorder are probably less well developed than for other addictions, but if people have a family history of addiction of any kind, then it makes them more likely to have another substance use disorder, which could be cannabis.

#4939. BMW iX5 hits up to 460 kW during first public fast-charging demo

With up to 460 kW DC fast charging, the new BMW iX5 can add up to 170 miles in just 10 minutes. BMW proved it during a live public event for the first time.

BMW’s new electric vehicles are a step change from its previous-generation EVs. Based on its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system with 800V technology, the setup delivers up to a 30% increase in driving range and charging speeds compared to the Gen5 system.

In addition to new, highly efficient electric motors, the Gen6 eDrive uses new batteries with cylindrical cells that BMW says provide 20% greater energy density than the Gen5 prismatic cells.

To prove just how fast it can charge, BMW put the new iX5 50 xDrive to the test during an international media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW, even slightly higher than the 460 kW that BMW reported.

BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the 144 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

While the results are impressive, 460 kW is the peak rate, not the sustained rate during the entire charging session. Either way, it’s still impressive and quick enough to get you back on the road quickly.

The vehicle averages over 280 kw across the 10%-80% range. That is a sustained rate faster than the peak charging of most vehicles. The 450 miles of range means it will add 315 EPA miles in less than 22 min. Impressive for any vehicle available in the US.

Plus, the US does not have the hardware to support 460 kW charging. Alpitronic supplied the hardware, and the demo was at an IONNA charger.

BMW will launch the 2027 iX5 60 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800. Official EPA figures are still pending, but BMW estimates the iX5 will offer up to 435 miles of range with a 144 kWh battery.

It’s powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, which BMW says enables it to go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.

The new iX5 is BMW’s first all-electric vehicle produced in the US. BMW is set to begin production at its Plant Spartanburg by the end of the year.

#4937. Rivian now #2 US EV brand, up from #10, as Big Auto marginalizes itself

Rivian is now the #2 EV brand in the US, up from 10th last year, taking Chevrolet’s spot as almost every other automaker tries to slow down the inevitable transition to electric cars.

In the last year, the US electric car market has been… volatile, to say the least.

Q3 2025 saw a huge sales jump, in an advance of an effort by US republicans to inflate the price of EVs by $7,500.

So, looking forward to this year, it was inevitable that we would see a large drop in sales in Q3, since records were set in last Q3.

Sure enough, as sales numbers came in, most brands were down. This is to be expected after incentive expiry – though EV sales have been steadily recovering in the intervening months.

Part of the reason for that recovery has been due to a lot of dumb oil conflicts around the world, causing oil prices to rise to record levels (helped by intentional policy decisions to push them even higher). As oil prices rise, the already-obvious case for electric transportation becomes all the more clear.

This has caused EV sales to shoot up in the rest of the world. Unfortunately, American access to affordable EVs has been restricted due to dumb tariffs and other barriers intended to keep Americans spending and polluting more.

EV sales could have been higher in the US, but the reason they’ve stayed depressed from previous levels isn’t due to consumer demand, but because automakers are almost universally refusing to make EVs, according to research from UC Davis.

There are a few exceptions, though. With Rivian as the standout among them.

According to Cox Automotive’s new Q3 sales report, almost every brand saw a decrease in EV sales in Q3, with Mercedes, Lexus, Toyota, Subaru, and Rivian as the exceptions.

Each of these brands have new models which helped to bring up sales. Toyota has its improved bZ and new C-HR, Lexus its new ES, Subaru its Trailseeker and Uncharted, Mercedes its CLA, and most importantly, Rivian has its R2.

Meanwhile, many of the brands with falling sales have cancelled models (even ones that were previously their best-sellers). Unsurprisingly, when Americans are not allowed to buy a car, they won’t buy it.

Rivian’s new R2 is a make-or-break car for the company, a much more affordable, smaller version of its R1S. It just started sales a few months ago, and Rivian hopes to ramp up production, aiming for the same market the Tesla Model Y is in.

The Model Y remains the US’ best-selling EV, but its sales went down year over year as well. Tesla has not so much retreated from EV production, more that its CEO is now spending more money to harm EVs than any other person on the planet. Even with Tesla’s nearly 20% drop in sales year over year, It’s still ahead of the rest of the pack.

But 2nd place used to be taken up by Chevy, which was proud of that fact. It has several capable EV offerings, including the newly-improved, affordable Chevy Bolt (which is, nevertheless, being cancelled next year). (GM is still second place if you combine all of its brands together, though, but if Rivian’s growth continues, that may or may not hold)

As car sales crater, the charging networks seem to be going all in on expanding the network. As an EV owner I’m delighted, road trips are getting much easier. Both the number of stalls and reliability is much improved from just 2-3 years ago. But I’m also puzzled - why are the charging networks so bullish? Why are they investing heavily when manufacturers are retreating? And is this going to continue? For example IONNA is expanding as fast as they can when the manufacturers that jointly own IONNA can’t seem to back away from the EV market fast enough. Is there something I’m missing that explains this dissonance? I sure hope in a few years we don’t look back on 2026 as the golden age of DCFC networks.

Last year, Rivian was all the way back in 10th place. But with its growth in sales and everyone else’s retreat, Rivian has now shot up to second place in Q3, selling more EVs in the quarter than anyone except for Tesla.

And that’s just at the start of R2 sales. Rivian only booked 3,456 units of the R2 in Q3, which is fewer than the number of R1S it sold. Given the R2’s much cheaper sticker price, once the company gets up to speed and starts offering lower-end ~$50k models, volume should be much higher than the ~$80k R1S – just as was the case with the Model X and Model Y.

And given the direction society is currently going, towards hopefully greater realization of the need to get off of unreliable, polluting, foreign sources of energy and onto cleaner, sustainable domestic ones, Rivian is positioning itself well while the rest of the auto industry seems ready to throw everything away and hand China the industry on a silver platter.

#4936. This Is Your Brain on Weed. It’s Actually Kind of Amazing.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

WHEN YOU USE weed, your brain kind of goes all over the place. You likely know about how marijuana can chill you out, make you forget yourself, and induce the munchies. But there are other fascinating ways that the drug can alter your mind.

When THC binds to receptors in your hippocampus, the compound disrupts signals and impairs memory. That’s why you may forget what you were saying mid-sentence or where you put your keys when stoned.

THC also binds to receptors in the amygdala, which can help you feel chill when high—and paranoid or anxious when you’re too high.

The back of the brain, the cerebellum, is important for balance, motor skills, and time perception. When THC gets involved, you might feel clumsier and as if time is slowing.

THC disrupts the prefrontal cortex, which oversees critical thinking, problem-solving, and processing information from your senses. As a result, you’re going to find it harder to multitask, feel more impulsive, and zone out.

THC also stimulates the release of feel-good dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. If you’re a chronic, heavy user, cannabis can dull dopamine response and potentially rewire circuitry within the nucleus accumbens, making you more susceptible to addiction.

Your prefrontal cortex and limbic system contribute to imaginative ideas. THC can bind to receptors in these regions and may reduce self-critical noise, allowing for greater free expression.

Scientists believe that the anterior cingulate cortex is central to the perception of pain, and THC seems to dampen its ability—in a good way.

There’s so much more going on in the world of weed and health. Read more here.

#4935. How This New Orleans Hotel Went From Former Haunted House to Chic Destination

The Greek Revival mansion that sits at the corner of Prytania Street and Jackson Avenue in New Orleans’ Garden District wouldn’t know “dull” if it came up and rang the doorbell. The 1857 building’s first owner was a cotton merchant who died of yellow fever. Another owner was fatally struck by lightning. Fast-forward to the 21st century, when a Tina Turner impersonator bought the property and turned it into Magnolia Mansion, a B&B with suites with names like Vampire Lovers’ Lair and Moulin Rouge. A former professional boxer and local politics kingmaker took over, but things fell apart around the time of the FBI’s raid on the property.

Oh, and the estate is said to be haunted.

The Whit's moody mahogany-paneled library

Named in its B&B era by USA Today as one of the top places in the nation “to sleep with a ghost” the magisterial Harris-Maginnis House earned a spot on the city’s ghost-tour circuit with an ever-mounting pile of lore. According to a spooky tour-operator website, guests at the B&B reported various eerie happenings over the years, such as the sensation of somebody tucking them in at night or a presence watching them while they slept. There were also rumblings of mysterious footsteps and slamming doors. Ghosts or no ghosts, the new team taking over the place found gothic-coded wall murals and dark purple velvet hanging at every turn.

Who you gonna call to give an old haunt a new design vernacular? Gretchen Trauth, CEO of the New Orleans investment firm behind the New Orleans hotel, rang up Jensen Logan and Katie Leblanc Killen of Logan Killen, a local design firm known for infusing spaces with a beguiling mix of polish and patina. “The goal was a hotel where nobody can quite tell whether a designer has touched it,” says Logan.

Breakfast room with Pierre Frey wallpaper

“We wanted it to feel very storied, like it’s been someone’s house for a long time,” adds Killen. “There are these layered histories imbued in the furnishings and the art and accessories.”

Named for poet Walt Whitman, who spent three months in New Orleans around the time of the home’s construction, the designers have reimagined the property with a romantic, lived-in, and curio-studded aesthetic that tempts guests to sit down and stay awhile. Architect Seamus McGuire of New Orleans firm Cicada helped navigate historical codes and redraw the map to capture some of the glamour that had drained away in recent years. His blueprint called for converting a trio of bedrooms into lounges. A mahogany-paneled library is now a gallery of antique dog portraits and a repository of volumes from local independent Faulkner House Books. “It’s dark and moody, and where you might want to have a cocktail or a whiskey,” Logan says of the clubby room. Bookworms might also gravitate to the sunroom’s banquette seating, one of the wicker chairs on the wraparound porch, or the breakfast room, a delightfully matchy-matchy enclave covered in Pierre Frey Les Colonnes wallpaper and curtains.

The hardest room to get right, say the designers, was the main lounge. “It’s a giant space that isn’t always in use, and can be tricky to give life to when it’s empty,” says Killen. Intended to serve as a great room by day and an atmospheric cocktail bar come evening, the team layered in elements such as blue paint that reads ethereal by day and warm by night, a custom grid carpet to add a sense of tailoring to the expansive area, and an intimate salon-style wall of works by Louisiana artists, including Robert Moreland and Mallory Page.

Another tightrope walk was the second-floor bar. Landmark rules forbid faking history a space never had, so the team went openly Deco instead. “What we don’t want is to put a contemporary bar into a very historic property,” says McGuire. “You can’t give a false sense of history to a space.”

It will probably come as little surprise that the bedrooms resist uniformity. In addition to the classically designed units, a quartet of cozy garden rooms has low ceilings and glossy oxblood walls; three cabana rooms feel airy, with bamboo beds and high ceilings. “It’s not meant to feel like everything was changed by the same person at the same time,” Killen says of the narrative that she and Logan have introduced to the New Orleans hotel.

As for the supposed ghosts, nobody’s heard boo.

#4933. Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings preview: flat revenue, falling profits

Tesla reports its third-quarter 2026 financial results tomorrow, October 21, after the market closes. The earnings call follows at 5:30 p.m. ET.

Wall Street expects revenue to come in flat and earnings per share to drop 10% from a year ago, even though Tesla just beat its own delivery consensus by more than 24,000 vehicles.

We already have the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2.1% from its all-time record of 497,099 in Q3 2025, but well above the 461,974 consensus Tesla compiled from 24 analysts.

It built only 464,391 vehicles during the quarter. So Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it produced, the second quarter in a row it has worked down inventory after building roughly 50,000 excess vehicles in Q1.

It’s still a two-car company. Model 3 and Model Y made up 478,237 of those deliveries, while “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi and what’s left of Model S and X) fell 48% year-over-year to 8,295 units.

Energy storage was the weak spot. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh, up 9.6% from 12.5 GWh a year ago, but well short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected and below the 14.2 GWh record it set in Q4 2025.

The Wall Street consensus calls for $28.06 billion in revenue, with the Estimize crowd a bit more bullish at $28.36 billion. Either way, that’s flat against the $28.1 billion Tesla reported in Q3 2025. Wall Street estimates range from $25.1 billion to $30.6 billion.

Flat isn’t as bad as it sounds. Q3 2025 was inflated by US buyers rushing to grab the $7,500 federal tax credit before it expired on September 30, 2025, so matching it without the credit would be a decent result.

But look at the sequential picture. Tesla posted $28.24 billion in revenue in Q2 2026 on 480,126 deliveries and 13.5 GWh of storage. Q3 had more of both, yet Wall Street is modeling slightly less revenue and Estimize only about $120 million more, which means both are baking in lower average selling prices.

Analysts expect non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.45, down 10% from $0.50 in Q3 2025. The Estimize consensus is a little higher at $0.48, and Wall Street estimates range from $0.30 to $0.70.

Take that number with a grain of salt. In Q2, Tesla came in at $0.33 against a $0.53 consensus, as its operating margin collapsed to 1.4%. Operating income fell 57% to $398 million while operating expenses jumped 47% to $4.35 billion.

Tesla has now missed the Street’s EPS estimate in two of the last four quarters. And its EPS has declined year-over-year in five of the last seven.

The number we’ll be watching first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits. It dropped to 16.3% in Q2 from 19.2% in Q1, which Tesla blamed on a $230 million warranty true-down and tariff relief that helped Q1 and didn’t repeat.

Regulatory credits won’t bail it out either. They brought in only $146 million in Q2, down 67% from a year earlier, and that pure-profit revenue keeps shrinking now that automakers no longer face federal CAFE penalties.

Then there’s cash. Tesla burned $1.09 billion in free cash flow in Q2 as capital expenditures more than doubled to $5.8 billion, and management guided to more than $25 billion in capex for 2026, with spending weighted to the second half. Another negative free cash flow quarter wouldn’t be a surprise.

Energy is worth a look too. The storage business ran a 20.4% gross margin in Q2, and Tesla says it expects the low-to-mid 20% range long term. With Q3 deployments missing estimates by more than 2 GWh, energy won’t offset much.

Tesla’s Say Technologies Q&A for the call closes today at 4 p.m. ET. It drew 832 questions from about 2,860 participants representing 3.85 million shares.

That’s more people than last quarter (about 1,710) but less than half the shares, which were 8.6 million in Q2.

Here are the top questions ranked by shares represented:

The auto business is flat. Deliveries are up 8.8% year-to-date at 1,324,681, which is a real recovery from two years of decline, but Q3 came in below last year and Tesla still sells almost nothing outside of Model 3 and Model Y.

Shareholders mostly listen to Tesla bulls like Cathie Wood. Notice the stock was up regardless of the news. As long as people like Wood say the stock may go up to $5000 per share, investors will continue to put in money.

So the quarter comes down to margins and spending. If auto margins ex-credits hold around 16% and opex stops climbing 40%+ a year, the Q2 miss was a one-off. If not, Tesla is spending more than $25 billion this year on AI, Optimus, Cybercab and chips while its core business barely breaks even at the operating level. That’s a car company funding a very expensive bet out of a shrinking profit pool.

And shareholders mostly don’t care. Look at the questions: Cybercab, FSD, Optimus, HW3. The top question about Tesla’s consumer lineup was a request for a van.

They are completely delusional, waiting for questionable new products to bring in money while watching their cash cows stop growing, something that was completely avoidable if Musk hadn’t bet the whole company on autonomy too early.
