#4932. Is This the Best Thanksgiving Turkey Recipe Ever?

A 5-Ingredient Brine. Cajun Rub. Two Hours in a Smoker. Perfection.

BACK IN 2021, D’Andre Carter was maxed out. The fine-dining chef had opened Soul & Smoke in Chicago, a barbecue-based food truck, and it incinerated his free time, which caused his weight to tick upward.

Then came the hypertension diagnosis, a wake-up call that he needed to act fast. He started jogging and eventually worked up to 60-minute runs five days a week, plus bodyweight exercises.

His diet now is loaded with lean protein (salmon, chicken) and nutrient-dense smoothies. He’s down 20 pounds from 220, his hypertension is in check, and he’s motivated. “Living healthy gives me the stamina to manage a busy life, be present for my family, and lead in the kitchen,” Carter says.

That means cooking well, for everyone, and especially on Thanksgiving, when he turns to this way-more-delicious holiday feast.

“This is my go-to method for a juicy, flavorful whole turkey—perfect for holidays or any gathering,” says Carter. “It’s all about the prep, the brine, and that smoke.”

1. In a large pot, stir 8 quarts of warm water with 1 cup of kosher salt, plus the sugar, onion, garlic, and thyme, until dissolved. Chill till cool, submerge the turkey in the liquid, and brine in the fridge overnight.

2. Remove the turkey from the brine, pat it dry, and rub all over with the olive oil. Season with the rub and 1 Tbsp coarsely ground black pepper.

3. Preheat a kamado smoker (like a Big Green Egg) or arrange a grill for indirect cooking at 350°F. Add the wood chunks. Place the turkey on the grill, breast side up, tucking in the wings underneath. Smoke, lid closed, for 1 hour, open the lid, baste the bird with the butter, and close the lid. Smoke until the internal temp reaches 170°F in the thickest part of the thigh, another 1 to 2 hours. Let the turkey rest for 30 minutes before carving. Feeds 10, with leftovers

The key to amazing barbecued anything is in the spice blend. This one works great on turkey, but also chicken and vegetables.

In a bowl, mix ¼ cup smoked paprika, 2 Tbsp kosher salt, 2 Tbsp garlic powder, 2 Tbsp onion powder, 2 tsp ground black pepper, 2 tsp dried thyme, 2 tsp dried oregano, 1 tsp cayenne pepper (adjust to taste), 1 tsp ground white pepper, and 1 tsp brown sugar. Makes roughly ¾ cup

#4930. This Shell-Shaped Villa Has Mediterranean Views and a Windswept Feel

When designer Federica Gosio talks about this project in Sardinia, she describes it as “an arch over the sea.” Gosio—who leads the firm bearing her name and is also a cofounder of Studio MILO—explains, “the truly unique aspect of this home is its ability to adapt to its surroundings, the sea, and nature.” Overlooking the bay of Porto Rafael, an area on the island’s northern coast famous for its remote location and its scenic beauty, the house resembles a seashell.

The villa looks like a white shell that has emerged from the sea to embrace the surrounding landscape .

There is no single guiding principle in Gosio’s design; instead, the shell-shaped villa embodies a capacity to adapt: “The aim is to give shape to ever-changing realities, integrating it with strength and grace into a larger context,” she says. It’s an approach that characterizes many of Gosio’s projects. This one springs from the rugged land where the home is located and pays homage to its setting through its design.

A custom-made bench follows the perimeter of the portico, wrapping around the space. At its center is a set of furnishings in wood and neutral-toned fabrics.

Working with Gosio, Alessandra Radaelli, the owner of this shell-shaped villa, created an organic, sculptural retreat. “We decided to honor the design legacy of Rafael Neville,” she says, referring to the founder of Porto Rafael. That meant “favoring a harmonious approach in which architecture blends with the landscape.”

Interior designer Federica Gosio on the terrace of this unique and intriguing villa.

The villa is characterized by curved lines and pure white surfaces that also have a textured quality. Rattan and straw accents add warmth to the space.

The home’s pointed arches, organic geometries, and natural materials were inspired by the earth and the sea. “The minimalist spaces were designed to embrace the sunlight, the wind, and the slow rhythm of island life,” Gosio explains. “It’s a project that interprets the Mediterranean in a contemporary way through a refined balance of memory, nature, and design.”

Every corner of this villa blends seamlessly with its surroundings: In this outdoor space, the shapes soften and the lines curve. At the center is a white rattan lounge set.

With its soft curves, the home feels as if it has been shaped by the winds that blow across Sardinia. During the winter, the Mistral here is powerful, sweeping across the island and reshaping the landscape. It looks almost as if the same process has taken place both inside and outside the villa. The reality is that this effect was a deliberate design choice to soften the edges of the villa and smooth out its different volumes.

This semicircular arch draws one’s gaze to the sea. In the foreground are two coffee tables by Mogg. In the background, on a terrace, rattan armchairs complement the organic curves of the seaside architecture.

Both inside and out, the villa is a whitewashed structure that follows the contours of the land. Gosio and her team have done away with straight lines, opting instead for a softer silhouette. The signature element of the home is undoubtedly the pointed arch, used for both the villa’s doors and its hallways. “The soft volumes, textured surfaces, and carefully placed rocks guide the visitor toward the entrance with its hand-brushed, iron arched door, custom-designed by Daniele Mingardo,” Gosio says.

The property’s garden is an idyllic green expanse leading down to the sea with junipers and various plants native to the Mediterranean framing the villa.

Interior designer Federica Gosio (on the left) and homeowner Alessandra Radaelli.

Surrounding the home are acres of land covered in lush Mediterranean vegetation leading down to the sea, with the route including green terraces and social spaces, including the panoramic pool and an outdoor kitchen. The feeling is that of an earthly Eden planted in a corner of Sardinia.

The organic arch reveals a living space featuring an Asawa sofa by Secolo, Dune side tables by Mogg, and a vintage rattan pendant lamp purchased on the Pamono website. The Paysage II rug is by Atelier Février, the blue ceramic Anfora Anulare vase is by Walter Usai, and the cups and saucers are by LR Ceramics.

The goal of respecting and celebrating the villa’s setting is also reflected in the colors and materials used throughout the home. “The white walls, the floors in Orosei marble with a bush hammered finish and ‘broken edges,’ and the organically shaped furnishings come together to create a measured and well-proportioned design, inspired by the neutral and warm tones of the soil here,” Gosio says.

Access to the kitchen is also through a large, sweeping arch. The custom oak cabinets are paired with WA ceramic tiles by Decoratori Bassanesi on the wall. The table, which resembles a sculpture, is the Luna Elíptica by La Nena.

Orosei stone, which is found on the coast of Sardinia, not only forms the floors but also the sinks (both indoor and outdoor), a clear example of how the island was integrated into the design. Rounding out the composition is a selection of vintage rattan pieces and sculptural creations by Pretziada, a creative design practice based in Sardinia, and its artisans. Nothing is left to chance and every element contributes to the home’s exquisite design and its appealing composition.

At the center of the dining area, which overlooks the outdoor space, is a Luna Elíptica table by La Nena. Next to it is a Lia Chair by Chiara Andreatti and Pierpaolo Mandis for Pretziada, a piece that is both handcrafted and contemporary, with roots in traditional Sardinian design. The Holden Linear Pendant Uplight is from Porta Romana. On the table are several ceramic pieces by LR Ceramics.

The infinity-edge pool blends seamlessly into the villa’s architecture. Alongside it is a sundeck surrounded by lush green foliage and aromatic plants.

The outdoor spaces in this villa are extensions of its interior. Wooden furnishings with a distinct nautical flair are set amid breathtaking green spaces with ocean views. On the table is a Mini Geen-A lamp by Kartell.

A custom outdoor kitchen with views of the sea. The sink is made of Orosei marble.

The pool has views of the sea and sunsets.

The primary bedroom, with its organic lines, overlooks the pool and, beyond it, the sea. The custom headboard is upholstered in a striped fabric. Next to it is a Holden Wall Light from Porta Romana.

In the guest room, the custom headboard sets the tone. Next to it is a pendant lamp with a rattan Braided Lampshade-Bottle by Ferm Living. Atop a stone nightstand, a vase by LR Ceramics.

In this bath, Totem tiles from the Nok collection by 41zero42 add texture to the wall. The sink is by Catalano, and the faucets are from the Sirius series by Rubinetterie Stella.

This bath, with its rich textural quality, is defined by the wall-mounted sink in Orosei stone paired with a Roma faucet set by Rubinetterie Stella.

This room evokes traditional Sardinian design with a custom headboard that’s a mosaic of shapes and neutral tones, upholstered in Zinc’s Cubilete Natural fabric. The Holden Wall Light is from Porta Romana, as is the Huxley Jordan Wall Light reading lamp.

#4929. A parking giant with 5,700 sites is taking on apartment EV charging

Apartment and condo residents could get more places to plug in their EVs without their buildings needing a costly electrical upgrade. LAZ Parking and EverCharge are launching a charging service that shares available power among vehicles – an approach the companies say can support up to five times as many charging ports on the same power supply.

The new service, LAZ Multifamily EV Charging Powered by EverCharge SmartPower, is available across LAZ’s US-wide footprint. EverCharge is a wholly owned subsidiary of indiGOtech, which goes by GO.

For anyone who lives in an apartment or condo, getting a charger installed can involve more than just choosing a parking space. The apartment building’s electrical capacity has to accommodate EV charging, and upgrading the infrastructure can make the project expensive before anyone plugs in.

EverCharge’s SmartPower manages charging output in real time based on how much electricity vehicles need and how much power the site has available. That gives property owners a way to install more chargers within their existing electrical limits, the company says.

The approach spreads the available power across charging vehicles as demand changes. The potential benefit is that more residents can plug in where they already park, with less need for expensive electrical work.

LAZ operates around 2.1 million parking spaces at 5,700 locations in the US and Canada. EverCharge already operates more than 10,000 charging ports at over 1,000 apartment and condo properties, serving more than 50,000 registered drivers.

LAZ says the venture expands its charging network to 25,000 ports across North America. That figure describes its expanded network; the announcement doesn’t set a target or timeline for new apartment and condo installations.

The big economy parking lot at LAX has a similar system. Basically every spot has an EV charger. When you park, you enter into the app how long you're going to be parked. The charger than prioritized/deprioritizes your charging speed and current draw based on that.

So a car parked there for a week-long vacation can happily trickle-charge over those days, while someone parking for a quick up-and-back to San Francisco can leave with a full battery. And obviously ICE cars won't tie up any current at all.

The rollout will use EverCharge’s EVO3 Level 2 chargers. The companies haven’t disclosed resident charging prices or named the first properties getting installations. Beyond residential charging, they also plan to explore charging and battery swapping for commercial fleets, ride-hailing, and delivery services.

#4926. Mercedes’ new GLC 400 EV crushes range estimates, driving nearly 400 miles

The new 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic EV has an EPA-estimated range of up to 331 miles, but in the real world, it will likely go even farther.

Electric vehicles are becoming more efficient thanks to advances in batteries, drive units, and more, enabling longer driving ranges and faster charging.

The new 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic EV has an EPA-estimated range of up to 331 miles, which is more than enough for at least a few days of commuting on average.

In everyday driving conditions, it may drive much farther than its official numbers suggest. During Edmunds’ real-world range test, the GLC 400 EV drove 392 miles, or 18% more than its EPA estimate.

An extra 61 miles of range is huge. It could add another two, three, or even more days of commuting between charges.

The electric GLC was also more efficient, consuming just 28.4 kWh per 100 miles, about 14% less than the EPA’s official 33 kWh per 100 miles.

Mercedes’ new GLC outperformed most of the competition in the real-world range test. The 2027 Volvo EX60 P10 AWD traveled 352 miles, the 2025 Cadillac Optiq covered 339 miles, and the 2027 Audi Q6 E-Tron Prestige managed 337 miles.

The Edmunds real-world range test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions.

It consists of 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set on auto at 72 degrees.

While charging speeds weren’t tested, the GLC 400’s 94 kWh battery supports DC fast charging up to 330 kW. Mercedes says it takes about 22 minutes to charge from 10% to 80%.

One thing is for certain: electric cars are quickly becoming more efficient with faster charging and longer driving range.

Several articles have implied that a tested EV has "blown past its EPA estimate." Not really. Edmunds uses a slower average speed for their tests than EPA. Other testers evaluate highway mileage runs, and guess what, they fall well short of their EPA test.

These results are exactly what one should expect.

The number of electric cars offering 300 miles or more of EPA-estimated range has grown from just 1 model in 2016 (the Tesla Model S 90D) to around 60 by the end of 2026.

Several new 2027 models are now pushing closer to 400 miles of EPA range on a single charge. A recent BMW Group study found that Americans want more range than what they actually need.

The study found that 73% say 75 miles or less would cover their daily driving routine, while 42% want at least 300 miles before considering an EV. Only 18% of respondents said they wanted 400+ miles.

Did the 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC catch your attention? See if you can find one close to you (find what’s available nearby).

#4924. 10 Best Airbnbs in London With Brilliant Design (2026)

If London excels at anything, it’s lodgings with soul—from the silver-service glamour of Claridge’s to the shiny new scenes of At Sloane. But these days, it’s the city’s next generation of stays—creative, design-led rentals that might include a sweet stay tucked into a mews, a contemporary warehouse with exposed brick, or a period town house on a leafy street—that capture the true spirit of living like a local. In a place where nightly rates can soar well into four figures, claiming your own corner of the city feels more like the move. Here are the London Airbnbs where you can carry on like a local—homes that are made for sinking back into after a morning finding the best coffee or after a late night in Soho.

Perks: Sauna, sound system, fully-equipped kitchen, curated book selection, washer and dryer, centrally located near St. Pancras train station

Tucked away on a quiet corner in Islington, this three-story, Japanese-inspired stay is filled with wabi-sabi design moments you’ll want to steal for your own space. Guided by a minimal color palette, light-toned wood weaves cohesion throughout the interiors, which are outfitted with architectural details and decor accents. On cloudless days, sunlight bathes the upper levels, giving the wood flourishes a warm glow. The main living area trades a traditional sofa for tatami mats, where you can perform traditional tea ceremonies or simply enjoy a morning matcha. In the upstairs bedroom, camouflaged closets and drawers surround a grounded bed frame, while a freestanding tub placed right in front of the sleeping arrangements invites you for a relaxing soak.

The downstairs kitchen serves a helping of maximalism with its striking red marble center island and coordinating stove backsplash. Just steps away from the refrigerator, a hidden walk-in shower, sauna, and spare bathroom are discreetly tucked away. The owners describe this home as a “domestic gallery,” but its beauty doesn’t make it any less liveable. “Every detail is thoughtfully considered,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “A Space Residence reimagines mundane fixtures into modern design moments that make you feel like you’re living in art. Relaxing in the tub with a good book, enjoying a slow morning watching television in the kitchen, or taking a steam in the sauna are just a few ways the days will quickly pass in this lovely home away from home.” From $549 per night.

King or double-sized mattresses in each of the minimally designed bedrooms provide the perfect respite after long days spent visiting London sights like the nearby Japanese-inspired Kyoto Garden and Fukushima Garden, as well as Hyde Park and Kensington Palace just a short walk east. #4923. 4 Workout Strategies This Over-50 Trainer Uses to Keep Building Muscle

Use his guidance so you can train hard and hurt less.

THE MUSCLE-BUILDING NARRATIVE after age 50 isn’t pretty. According to doomers online, your testosterone levels are falling, your energy levels are in massive decline, and everything seems to throw your back out.

But contrary to popular belief, you can still muscle up. And Bryan Krahn, 53 years old and as strong as he’s ever been, is proof. The trainer, who created MH’s Max Muscle at 50 workout program, still works out four or five days a week and has maintained a muscular 210-pound physique..

That doesn’t mean he trains exactly like he did when he was in his 20s. Instead, over the last three decades, he’s made a series of adjustments, shifting his fitness priorities (much less bench pressing) and experimenting with new gym ideas. All that trial-and-error helped Krahn develop these four critical post-50 training principles, which will allow you to push your muscle-building limits for decades to come without crushing your body. He discussed these ideas (and much more) on MH’s Strong Talk podcast.

LIKE MOST GUYS, Krahn relied on dumbbells and barbells for years. But about a decade ago, those exercises started to hurt his joints. He has since shifted his focus to training that minimizes his risk of getting hurt. He is quick to note this isn’t about being overly cautious—avoiding injury is not the same as training scared.

Part of the fix for Krahn involved taking a little bit of time off. The other part: He headed to a section of the gym that guys often forget about: the machine area. Because yes, dumbbells and barbells and kettlebells seem to build more “functional” strength (so the narrative goes). But as you get older, those tools don’t always work as well with your joints. “Within four or five months, I have no pain, and I’m strong on these machines,” Krahn says. “Cables are indispensable as you get older.”

Machines allow you to focus on doing movements along very fixed tracks, and that lets you concentrate on generating the maximum amount of force with your muscles. That’s a key mechanic for growth. “And if you’re a beginner, generating that force isn’t always easy with free weights,” says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. “Inserting one machine exercise in your routines near the end can insure you get a chance to push your limits just a bit.”

Two machines to consider: A cable row machine, which blasts your back, and the leg press machine, which ensures you can challenge hamstrings, glutes, and quads with relatively heavy load.

A bonus: Experimenting with machines just may reignite your passion for the gym, too. Krahn says the machines allow him to enjoy his workouts—much like he did in his 20s. “I love going to the gym again,” he says.

FROM BARBELL BENCH presses to back squats to barbell deadlifts, some lifts in the gym are so popular and widespread, they might feel mandatory. But no—Krahn says you don't have to commit to any of them.

Krahn learned that when training arms. Yes, he loved skull crushers, a triceps exercise that can be notoriously tough on the elbows. But he swapped in triceps pressdowns and still built the muscle he was chasing. He did the same with his biceps work, swapping out supinated dumbbell biceps curls for hammer curls. "As soon as something feels off," he says, "let's try a variation."

Exercise physiologist and strength coach Dr. Pat Davidson agrees. Most lifts that guys think are mandatory can easily be replaced. "So many people just get emotionally attached to an exercise," Davidson says. "Don't marry an exercise."

Krahn says machines are especially valuable here, too. "It's so difficult to get hurt (on machines)," he says. "You can kind of unleash that side of yourself and really push into failure."

Major lesson: The moment you feel pain in your joints, consider finding a substitute lift for the exercise that's caused you pain. Don't wait.

THESE DAYS, KRAHN thinks about building more than muscle. He also wants to maintain his body’s ability to be powerful. What does it mean to be powerful? Muscles produce force—but they also need the ability to produce that force very quickly, which happens whenever you jump, hop, or begin to run.

And sure, plyometric exercises can train power. But once you’re in your 50s, your body can’t always absorb that pounding. That’s why Krahn loves sled pushes. He uses the move as a warmup, especially on upper body days when he’s focused on a variety of push activities. Pushing a weighted sled is a move that can build glutes, quads, and hamstrings, and light up your core. It also quietly trains something called triple-extension, the act of straightening your knee, hip, and ankle joints all at once—which is a key to running and jumping.

The best part of a sled push, Davidson says: You get to build power without much injury risk. “Anytime you’re in a forward lean acceleration posture, it's much safer,” Davidson says. “It’s almost a Smith machine of running.” Consider doing two to three sets of 30-second sled pushes to start your next workout.

SHORT ON TIME? If Krahn has only 15 minutes in a day, he’ll walk. It’s a non-negotiable in his life. “I get a lot done in that 15 minutes,” he says. “I don’t lift weights every day, but I walk every day.”

There are a lot of reasons to add walking into your daily routine. For Krahn, walking gives him the mental reprieve to step away from his responsibilities and keep his mind refreshed. Walking also keeps your body moving, limiting your sedentary time.

At 50, it’s not always about going hard or pushing or limits. Walking keeps your body moving in a joint-friendly manner, even when you're fatigued (while sneaking in some light calorie-burn, too). Daily walking also helps to lower the risk of heart disease, a concern at any age but especially for older adults.

“Right now, that’s the number one killer in the US,” Mario Mejia, PT, DPT, physical therapist at Next Play Physical Therapy & Performance, previously told MH. “Heart disease can happen anytime but as we age, physiologically there are differences in the heart, lungs, and bone structure.

Above all, Krahn's tips provide a template for how to keep building muscle and lose fat into your 50s and beyond. And Krahn's full Max Muscle at 50 program delivers even more guidance. Check it out here.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

#4919. Raw Denim vs. Regular Denim: Which Is Actually Worth Buying?

Here’s what to know about both kinds of jeans.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I COME FROM the denim era where streetwear juggernauts like FUBU and Rocawear reigned supreme, along with mall favorites like Abercrombie & Fitch and Hollister. I was in my preteens rocking all these clothing brands and you couldn’t tell me their baggy-stacking-at-the-shoe jeans weren’t the flyest on the market. Since I began working as a fashion editor, I’ve practically worn every pair of jeans in the denim universe. Slim, relaxed, stretch, washed, distressed—you name it, I’ve probably tried it. I’ve even tried my hand at denim-making in Japan, the mecca of old-school, high-quality denim, where I produced my own pair of selvedge jeans. Denim is one of those rare items in a guy’s wardrobe that never goes out of style.

And after years of being in the menswear space, I’ve gotten familiar with the nuances that distinguish one kind of denim from the next. Two worth knowing are regular denim and raw denim. Raw denim usually looks darker, stiffer, and more uniform in color, while regular denim has a softer feel and a more broken-in appearance with visible fading or whiskering from factory washing and finishing. Those differences also affect how each pair feels when you first put it on and how it changes over the years. Here’s what to know about both and which one deserves a spot in your rotation.

Regular jeans are usually made by weaving cotton yarn into denim, then cutting fabric into patterns and sewing them together to create the finished garment. These jeans have already gone through washing or finishing treatments to soften the fabric and give them that broken-in look, so you don’t have to spend weeks waiting for them to feel comfortable. If I want to throw on a pair of jeans and get on with my day, this is the kind I’m reaching for. I also like that you can find them in practically every fit and wash, whether you’re after a clean, dark indigo pair or something faded and lived-in. Most everyday options from brands like Levi’s and Wrangler run roughly $40 to $100, while designer and premium styles can cost considerably more. For me, prewashed denim makes the most sense when you want that comfortable feel from the jump. There’s nothing wrong with skipping the break-in period and getting straight to the good part.

I like raw denim because you get to see how jeans change the more you wear them. Unlike prewashed jeans, raw denim typically hasn’t been washed after the dyeing and manufacturing process, so it typically arrives stiff, dark, and pretty rigid. One thing to watch out for, though, is dye transfer. Indigo can rub off onto lighter-colored clothes, shoes, and other materials, including suede. I’ve had this happen before, so I'd be mindful of what you wear with a fresh pair. But that’s part of the appeal for denim enthusiasts. As you wear it, the fabric softens and develops fades and creases based on how you move, sit, and live in your jeans. You’re essentially breaking them in yourself, which makes the finished look feel uniquely yours. Prices can start around $60 to $100 for entry-level options and climb to $150 to $300 or more for premium denim, particularly Japanese-made styles. I’ll admit, the break-in period takes some patience, but if you enjoy watching your jeans evolve over time, raw denim is worth considering.

Raw denim and selvedge denim get lumped together all the time, but they actually refer to different things. Raw denim describes the fabric’s finishing state: It’s typically sold without a post-production wash that softens the fabric or creates a faded look. Selvedge, on the other hand, refers to how the denim is woven, creating a clean, self-finished edge you can often spot by rolling up the cuff. You can have raw selvedge denim, washed selvedge denim, or raw denim that isn’t selvedge at all. Having made my own pair of selvedge jeans in Japan, I’ve seen firsthand how the construction differs. Once you know what to look for, the distinction is pretty easy to spot.

At the end of the day, I don’t think you need to drop $300 on raw denim to dress well. After years of working in menswear, I’ve learned that a higher price tag doesn’t automatically make something the right choice for your wardrobe. I’ve seen guys look just as good in an affordable pair of Levi’s as they do in premium Japanese denim. What matters more is finding comfortable jeans that fit your body and work with the clothes you already own. I’m always going to appreciate the quality craftsmanship behind a great pair of raw denim, but there’s no single right way to wear jeans. I think every guy should have one dependable pair, whether that’s raw or prewashed. But ultimately, like most things in style, it comes down to personal preference—and knowing what works for you.

#4917. The 8 Best Natural Deodorants for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sticks that are gentler on your skin and the environment.

SUMMER HEAT MAY be gone, but you still need deodorant. While soaps and body wash rinse away sweat and grime, deodorant keeps odor at bay throughout the day by masking funky smells and killing odor-causing bacteria. So, it’s a crucial part of the defense—no matter the season. If you have sensitive skin or prefer eco-conscious products, natural deodorant is your best bet.

Traditional deodorants use ingredients that may irritate skin or disrupt your body’s natural sweat response, like parabens, phthalates, or, most notably, aluminum. While the FDA does list aluminum as a safe ingredient to be used in deodorants or antiperspirants, to be clear, those with sensitive skin can still find it irritating.

This is because the ingredient can cause inflammation leading to itchiness and rash, as well as worsening dry skin conditions like eczema, says dermatologist Dr. Anna Chacon, MD, FAAD. Not to mention, aluminum can inhibit the body’s natural sweat response by actively plugging pores with heavy metals that stop sweat from being excreted, she says.

Still, there is also a lot of noise out there regarding aluminum contributing to Alzheimer’s disease or cancer, but none have been substantiated. Still, natural alternatives skip this risk and instead rely on plant-based ingredients like essential oils, probiotics, and starches to combat odor and moisture.

Quick reminder: Deodorants do not block sweat; they mask body odor. Only an antiperspirant will do this, but there are no natural antiperspirants, as aluminum is required to plug sweat glands. So, natural deodorants are used as an alternative to both. Plus, they tend to be better for the environment by often using biodegradable ingredients or eco-friendly packaging to reduce waste and plastic pollution.

With all of this in mind, it’s fair to wonder why natural deodorants aren’t the norm. Well, these products have a bit of a bad reputation when it comes to their ability to last as long as traditional aluminum-filled options. While this does hold true for many natural deodorants, there are options on this list that last just as long, and in the case of Ursa Major Hoppin' Fresh Natural Deodorant, which lasts well over 24 hours, outperforms most traditional deodorants.

Salt and Stone incorporates hyaluronic acid and seaweed extract in its natural deodorant to eliminate bad odor, prevent underarm darkening, and deliver intense hydration, which is crucial for preventing funky smells, maintaining health skin, and ensuring proper sweat gland functioning. Not to mention, these ingredients will keep you smelling fresh from morning to night.

While most deodorants (natural and otherwise) have alcohol, which can cause blocked pores, irritation, and dryness, this vegan option leaves it out of the formula. But what really separates Salt and Stone from other brands is its killer natural fragrances.

The santal and vetiver scent smells so good; I’ve often worn it in lieu of cologne. This fresh, subtle sandalwood smell lasts too—all day. The lightweight formula glides on smoothly and soothes my skin. It’s the only natural deodorant I’ve tried that straight up outperforms many of my go-to standard sticks.

It never stains, never aggravates my skin, and rarely needs to be reapplied (only after working out or something especially sweaty). Whether you’re looking for a natural deodorant that smells great or one that’ll keep you protected from odor, Salt and Stone is the best option.

Schmidt’s is a natural deodorant that skips the common bacteria-absorbing and odor-neutralizing baking soda, but still delivers. Packed with skin-friendly ingredients like magnesium and charcoal, it glides on smoothly, dries to a matte finish, and works for virtually all skin types, including sensitive. I have sensitive pits and have faced zero irritation when using this stuff.

The crisp citrus and spearmint scent feels fresh without being overpowering. With just a couple of swipes, you get all-day odor control. I’ll put this on after a pre-work shower and still smell it the next morning when I wake up. Pro tip: Warm the stick briefly against your skin before applying for a smoother glide. While it won’t block sweat, arrowroot and magnesium help absorb moisture and fight funk.

Ursa Major Hoppin' Fresh Natural Deodorant is one of the most reliable natural options out there. It goes on smooth, never stains, and keeps me smelling fresh with its crisp peppermint eucalyptus scent. The formula does use baking soda, so those with sensitive skin may want to look elsewhere. However, it also includes kaolin clay, which absorbs sweat, and hops—just like your favorite beer—to fight odor by neutralizing the growth of odor-causing bacteria (but not sweat, to be clear).

When I use this stick, my skin stays calm and clear. I’ve found that it can ward off odor in the midst of the sweatiest, stickiest summer outings, like a long run or a day at the beach. Plus, I’ve had a Hoppin' Fresh stick last over three months. This thing’s a legit money saver.

Most natural deodorants, understandably, use a lot of fragrance to help mask odor. Somehow, this fragrance-free version neutralizes stink without the aid of added scent. It could be the probiotics in the formula that help to maintain good (non-stinky) bacteria. Or it could be voodoo, who knows? This Hume helped keep B.O. at bay during even the hottest days outside. While it doesn't stop sweat like an antiperspirant, of course, the fragrance-free formula does keep you smelling fresh and clean, somehow. It’s just more like that fresh-out-of-the-shower clean, rather than cologned-up clean.

Some natural deodorants ask you to change your routine—they don’t apply as easily as the traditional ones you’re used to. Native, however, goes on smoothly and doesn’t need to be warmed up or applied with your fingers. This clean vanilla and sandalwood scent is fresh without smelling fake.

The warm, woodsy fragrance is clean and masculine without being overpowering. It goes on cleanly, without any residue, thanks to the twist-up stick. Often natural deodorants, they have a looser texture, but this is the closest to the feel of a traditional stick.

So, if you’re going natural for the first time, it’s the perfect place to start. The included arrowroot and tea tree oil will leave you feeling fresh, and I’ve had one stick last about two months with daily use. This is another one with baking soda, however, so those sensitive might see a reaction (though I didn’t!).

Fighting tough stains can be, well, tough. Enter Malin and Goetz's natural deodorant. With a unique combination of citronellyl and eucalyptus extract, this transparent formula won't leave any traces of residue on your favorite garments. It’s not the strongest deodorant, to be clear, as it will start to fade around the 12-hour mark.

But the cooling scent lasts longer than others that need to be reapplied often. Plus, the lightweight application goes on clear and seemingly evaporates in seconds. I’ve worn black T-shirts at the same time as wearing this deodorant without a trace.

Humble Brands Plastic-Free deodorant is made with just four clean ingredients plus essential oils, and it skips all the junk: no aluminum, parabens, dyes, or synthetic fragrances. The Mountain Lavender scent is earthy and calming, though it may be a bit too strong for those who don’t love an essential oil scent.

What really sold me, however, is the packaging—completely plastic-free, biodegradable, and even the ink is plant-based. Sure, it keeps me dry and odor-free all day, but I also feel good knowing it’s as gentle on my skin as it is on the planet. It’s no wonder Jason Momoa chose Humble to help launch his first deodorant.

Read More: Inside Jason Momoa’s Humble Deodorant

No brand nails masculine, earthy scents quite like Dr. Squatch, and its natural deodorant is no different. The pine tar-scented option, especially, nails the peaceful fragrance of woods at dawn. In fact, it’s the closest I’ve gotten to the indescribable smell of waking up after a night camping in the Sequoia National Forest.

That being said, the deodorant isn’t confirmed to be entirely 100 percent natural. While every ingredient listed could be naturally derived, the brand only confirms 98 percent natural. Still, I never had a reaction with my sensitive skin, and there certainly isn’t any aluminum in the formula. While the application is clean and lightweight, Dr. Squatch also packs one of the longest-lasting scents on this list (up to 48 hours, in my experience).

Again, natural deodorants will never contain aluminum to block sweat. Instead, they use sweat-absorbing ingredients like arrowroot powder, clay, or tapioca starch to manage moisture without stopping sweat entirely. If you see aluminum listed, it’s not truly natural.

Many natural formulas include baking soda to fight odor and absorb wetness, but it can also irritate sensitive skin, causing redness or itching. For those with sensitive skin, baking soda-free options are a safer choice. Natural deodorants also feature soothing moisturizers like coconut oil or other plant-based oils, plus fragrances from essential oils to keep you fresh.

Most natural deodorants mask odor with either synthetic fragrances, like limonene (found in orange peels) and linalool (from plants like lavender and basil), or natural essential oils like lavender, tea tree, or lemon. Neither is inherently better, just comes down to what scent you’re into. But keep in mind that while stronger scents may last longer, there is no guarantee for better odor protection.

Many natural deodorants include extra ingredients to fight odor after the scent fades, including bacterial absorbents like arrowroot, cornstarch, potassium alum, or zinc. If you have sensitive skin, heavy fragrances can still cause irritation, so opt for lighter or unscented formulas.

If you’re going the natural deodorant route for environmental reasons, you’ll probably also want to look for cruelty-free options, which means that the product was not tested on animals. While many grooming products are tested on animals, natural deodorants often prioritize more ethical practices, choosing not to test on animals as part of their commitment to a clean, conscious lifestyle, Dr. Chacon says.

As a grooming editor who was raised on The Grateful Dead not far from Woodstock, I’m intimately familiar with natural, eco-friendly alternatives. For this story, I considered personal favorites and options with high ratings on major e-commerce sites like Amazon. Ultimately, I landed on over 20 natural deodorants to test throughout the past year.

I wore each for at least a week, judging scent, staying power, the way it felt on my skin, and how well they held up through workouts, stress, and overall sweat. From that hands-on testing, these are the eight best natural deodorants for men that actually perform.

The most common argument that natural deodorants are better for you is centered around aluminum. Some claim that aluminum is linked with Alzheimer’s disease, but older studies have been discredited, and there has been no discernible link found between aluminum and Alzheimer’s, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.

It’s also been suggested that aluminum can increase your risk of cancer, particularly breast cancer in women. Dr. Chacon says that more research to determine a concrete link between either is needed, but early studies showing greater aluminum buildup in the brains of Alzheimer’s sufferers is concerning.

There is also usually conversation around preservative parabens, which some claim are linked to cancer as well, and other chemical ingredients that natural deodorants omit from their formulas. While, again, no studies have proven that these ingredients are directly linked to illnesses like cancer, many people like to err on the side of caution.

Apart from all this, traditional deodorants often contain ingredients that can irritate skin, like certain kinds of alcohol or artificial fragrances. Most natural deodorants seek to solve this problem by using naturally derived ingredients that may be more gentle on the skin. The bottom line is that there is no evidence that natural deodorants are better for you than traditional deodorants or antiperspirants; some simply prefer them for their lifestyle and skin.

#4916. The 25 Best Places to Live in the US (2026-2027)

Each year U.S. News & World Report releases a list of the best places to live in the US. While typically these top-rated locales include a number of big players, like Miami and New York, in the most recent list, suburbs reign supreme and major metropolises are notably absent. To determine the best cities in the country, U.S. News considers a multitude of factors, including quality of life, the local job market, value for your money, and the place’s desirability. And while we agree that all these factors are important in determining where to live in America—which is also ranked on AD’s list of best countries to live in—we’d also throw access to art and design into the mix. That’s why we used the U.S. News list as a jumping-off point—zeroing in on the best places for design lovers among them.

Before you read on, a little more about the methodology:

Carmel, Indiana, earned the No. 1 spot on the U.S. News list thanks in large part to a healthy job market. In this suburb about 20 miles north of Indianapolis, unemployment is lower than the national average, and the median household income is higher: $144,615, compared with $83,181. Plus, Carmel packs on the Midwestern charm, with friendly residents, a walkable downtown, and safe neighborhoods. The schools are excellent here as well. Carmel High School landed on the U.S. News Best High Schools list. And though homes in Carmel are pricier than the national average ($477,625 compared with $359,870), you get plenty for the money.

U.S. News determines quality of life based on how satisfied residents are with their daily lives, considering factors such as crime rates, quality of education, quality and availability of health care, and commute times. Tamarac, Florida, ranked No. 1 for quality of life, with Palo Alto, California; Doral, Florida; and Bethesda, Maryland (included on our list below), right behind it. For those who want quality of life outside of the US, consider our list of the best countries for Americans to move to.

On a separate U.S. News list of The Most Affordable Places to Live in the US, Eagle Pass, Texas, took top honors. Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, landed in the top 20 (at spot 12) and is included on our list below. But within the Best Places to Live list, U.S. News examined each city’s median annual household income compared with home prices in the area. And as you’ll see below, good design and affordable real estate aren’t mutually exclusive. Average housing costs in Ankeny, Iowa; Pearland, Texas; Broken Arrow, Oklahoma; Sioux Falls, South Dakota; El Paso, Texas; Appleton, Wisconsin; Farmington Hills, Michigan; Oklahoma City, Oklahoma; and Cedar Rapids, Iowa, are below the national average, and all of these places have landed on our design-centric list.

We chose our top 25 from the U.S. News list based on access to museums, art, cultural institutions, and top-notch architecture. We also considered which cities best fuel creative energy and make the best places to live for designers, artists, and innovators.

Indiana is a highly celebrated state, claiming the first two spots on the U.S. News list with Carmel and Fishers. Texas also makes a number of appearances in the top 10, thanks to Flower Mound, Leander, Frisco, and Sugar Land. But in a separate U.S. News list of the Best States, the top honor goes to Utah, which earns high marks for its fiscal stability, infrastructure, and excellent education.

The Carmel Arts and Design District is at the heart of the suburb.

Anyone who regularly reads best-places-to-live lists will instantly recognize Carmel—this Indianapolis suburb is always a favorite. It has superb schools, low crime, and a thriving job market. It also has a buzzing Arts and Design District, with galleries, studios, locally owned shops, and public art and sculptures. Plus, the district is a major hub on the Indiana Glass Trail, a collection of artists and studios dedicated to the region’s rich history in glassmaking that stretches across eight counties in the Hoosier State.

A train station in Fishers that was later turned into a pedestrian walkway

Coming in just behind Carmel, Fishers ranks second for places to live in Indiana and second in the national ranking, according to U.S. News. And back in 2017, Money Magazine named it the best place to live in the country. Located about 30 minutes north of Indianapolis, Fishers consistently earns accolades for its safety, top-notch education system, and excellent outdoor attractions, including 100 miles of nature trails, 24 parks, and even an outdoor music venue—the Nickel Plate District Amphitheater. The city also packs a punch in terms of cultural offerings, most notably through The Fishers Art Center, where locals can take pottery, painting, and drawing classes, and explore contemporary art exhibitions.

As the name suggests, Flower Mound is rich in natural beauty, with nearly 1,000 acres of parkland; over 75 miles of trails for hiking, biking, and horseback riding; as well as proximity to two lakes: Lake Grapevine and Lake Lewisville. The town gets its name from the wildflowers—including Texas bluebonnets, pansies, and wild foxglove—that blanket its elevated town center. Flower Mound also has top-tier schools and easy access to major metropolitan areas. Dallas is just 28 miles southeast of town, and Fort Worth is 33 miles southwest. All of the above, plus high ranks in health care and a strong economy, helped Flower Mound earn the No. 1 spot on Livability’s list of Best Places to Live in 2025.

Ankeny is a fast-growing suburb of Des Moines.

The top spot to live in the Hawkeye State, according to U.S. News, is Ankeny, a suburb of Des Moines that began as a farming community—it’s even home to a 455-acre John Deere factory that’s been in operation since 1947. But these days, there’s more to Ankeny than just soybeans, corn, and tractors. The rapidly growing suburb has its fair share of cultural attractions too, including museums such as the Ankeny Area Historical Society Museum, the Iowa Aviation Heritage Museum, and the Ankeny Art Center. Both kids and adults can take classes in pottery, drawing, watercolors, and acrylics at the art center. That is, of course, when they’re not busy cycling the town’s 25-mile High Trestle Trail, which is an art attraction in itself. At night, Blue LED fixtures light up a bridge on the trail, creating a mesmerizing portal-like display. The glowing bridge was made possible by a public art grant, illustrating Ankeny’s commitment to culture in addition to first-rate schools, public parks, and a high standard of living.

Johns Creek, Georgia, is a suburb of Atlanta.

This Atlanta suburb landed in the top five on the U.S. News list (and in the top spot in last year’s ranking) thanks in large part to a healthy job market and a median household income of $163,653 (compared with the national median household income of $79,466). Additionally, the average commute time in Johns Creek is only 26 minutes. That proximity to the city also means access to Atlanta museums such as the Museum of Contemporary Art of Georgia and the High Museum of Art—the Southeast’s largest museum for visual art and features architecture by both Richard Meier and Renzo Piano. In Johns Creek itself, The Art Center is home to exhibits, classes, and workshops. Plus, public art—including various murals and sculptures—can be found in parks and along pedestrian trails around town. The town also has its own orchestra, the Johns Creek Symphony Orchestra.

Hoover Metropolitan Stadium in Hoover, Alabama

Alabama’s top place to live earns high marks for its affordability, with a lower cost of living compared with other similarly sized metro areas. The town, just 20 minutes south of downtown Birmingham, also has a great appreciation for preserving its architecture and parkland. In 1997, the city purchased the historic Aldridge estate, turning it into the Aldridge Gardens, a botanical garden that’s open to the public and offers yoga classes, art exhibits, and group tours of its remarkable hydrangea beds. The city also bestowed a Hoover Historical Society Marker upon its Park Avenue Historical District, a neighborhood with architecture that spans from the late 19th century to just after World War II. The district is home to the 1923 Bluff Park Elementary School, the 1889 Overseer’s House, and the 1910 Hale-Joseph House.

Like Hoover, Alabama, Rochester Hills has a low cost of living when you compare housing costs (an average of $388,231 vs. a national average of $359,870) and the median household income ($119,938 vs $83,181 nationally). This family-friendly town, located about 25 miles north of downtown Detroit, is also celebrated for its low crime rates, top-notch schools, and accessible health care—Henry Ford Rochester Hospital is here. The town also offers plenty to inspire art and design fans, including galleries like Rochester Fine Art Market, Subjectively Objective, and the Oakland University Art Gallery, which is in the neighboring city of Rochester.

This Austin suburb offers proximity to the state capital at a more affordable price. Here, the average housing cost is $495,712, compared with $581,402 in Austin, which is only a 30- to 45-minute drive away. Plus, the CapMetro Rail gives commuters a direct route to downtown on public transportation. Design-wise, Leander offers Texas Hill Country charm, more modern architecture, and even a master-planned community of midcentury-inspired homes. Starlight Village, where construction began about 10 years ago, is a community of homes that look like they could’ve been plucked straight from 1950s Palm Springs—butterfly roofs, orange doors, wood-paneled walls and all.

Located within North Carolina’s Research Triangle—the region that quite literally forms a triangle between Raleigh, Durham, and Chapel Hill, and their research-heavy universities (Duke, UNC-Chapel Hill, and NC State)—Cary is a desirable home for anyone interested in science and tech. The city is also ripe for residents wanting to live somewhere that embraces progressive urban design and planning. The town has even adopted a long-term plan called “Imagine Cary,” a comprehensive vision to guide growth through 2040 and create a sustainable urban-suburban lifestyle. Areas of focus under the plan include transportation, housing, shopping, and environmental initiatives. In addition to looking toward the future, the people of Cary actively preserve the past through notable restoration projects including the Page-Walker Arts & History Center, a former 19th-century hotel that’s now a hub for the arts, and the Nancy Jones House, a residence that dates back to 1803.

The Kresge Foundation headquarters in Troy, Michigan

If it was good enough for legendary architect Minoru Yamasaki, who designed the original World Trade Center, the city of Troy deserves a spot on our list. Yamasaki and his family lived in Troy for 25 years, and he operated his architecture firm, Yamasaki and Associates, out of the Detroit suburb. Locally, his firm designed their office building, the Columbia Center, and the Temple Beth El, a synagogue in nearby Bloomfield Hills. Beyond its architectural history, Troy is celebrated for its strong economy (global consumer intelligence company JD Power is headquartered here), excellent education system, and outdoor recreational offerings—the town has more than 1,000 acres of parkland.

Buffalo Creek Forest Preserve in Buffalo Grove, Illinois

The No. 1 place to live in the Land of Lincoln offers all the benefits of the ’burbs—great schools, low crime rates, and plenty of green space—with proximity to one of the country’s top cities for architecture: Chicago. Buffalo Grove is only about 30 miles northwest of the Windy City, giving its residents easy access to architectural marvels like the Frank Lloyd Wright–designed Robie House and the Wrigley Building, as well as world-class institutions such as the Art Institute of Chicago and the National Museum of Mexican Art. In Buffalo Grove itself, The Raupp Museum tells the history of the city, including an exhibit about Potawatomi life in the 1830s and a replica of an early-20th-century general store.

The Delores Fenwick Nature Center in Pearland, Texas

Affordable housing (the median housing cost is $319,753 compared to a national median of $370,489) and a low unemployment rate (3.6% compared to a national average of 4.5%) helped Pearland nab a spot in the top five on the U.S. News list. The city of 123,986 earns a place on our list because of its dedication to creative living. In 2024, it rolled out a Cultural Arts Master Plan aimed at fostering more cultural events and activities, developing a community arts and cultural center, providing more opportunities for children to participate in the arts, and creating a more vibrant downtown. Add to that, Pearland is only minutes from Houston, home to an Arts District with over 300 studio spaces for creatives of all kinds.

We like Broken Arrow—the fast-growing Tulsa suburb with a history tied to the Muscogee Creek Nation—for its buzzy arts and entertainment center, the Rose District (the name is a nod to the rosebushes that dotted the area’s original landscaping). The district is home to multiple art galleries, a performing arts center, a pavilion for a weekly farmers market, and The Museum Broken Arrow. A hub for local history, the museum gives visitors the chance to experience the town’s Main Street as it would have looked in the early 20th century, plus step inside a Civil War–era cabin. Meanwhile, U.S. News appreciates Broken Arrow for its job market, which is better than the national average, and its affordable housing—the median home value here is $251,667.

Lake Sammamish is a highlight of the Seattle suburb.

The ’burbs often get a bad rap for being nothing more than a series of strip malls, but that couldn’t be further from the truth in Sammamish—one of Seattle’s most desirable suburbs. Located about 30 minutes east of the city, Sammamish offers the best of both worlds: access to the metropolis’s tech-driven job market and jaw-dropping natural beauty. Lush forests, tranquil lakes, and the peaks of the Cascade Mountain Range are all baked into the scenery here. As such, boating, fishing, hiking, and cycling are popular activities among residents, as are visits to nearby Lake Sammamish State Park. Add to that, the city is celebrated for its excellent public schools, low crime rate, quality health care facilities, and culturally diverse community.

Called the “Technology City of the South,” Alpharetta is a hub for major corporations like ADP, Bakkt, and Aptean, and offers plenty of employment opportunities—some even say it has twice as many jobs as residents. The average household income is also higher here: $153,928 compared with $83,181 nationally. On the design front, Alpharetta is celebrated for its diverse residential styles, including Greek Revival, Queen Anne, and Craftsman homes in its historic downtown, as well as French country and European-inspired homes around Lake Windward.

Arlington Heights is located just northwest of Chicago.

Rumors abound that this northwest Windy City suburb might be the future home of the Chicago Bears’ stadium, a major perk for the area’s football fans. Other advantages of living in this city (technically an incorporated village) with a population of roughly 75,000 include access to public transportation (it’s only about 30 minutes to downtown Chicago by train), excellent public schools, a median housing cost that’s only slightly higher than the national average, and a super charming, walkable downtown. Arlington Heights is also home to the Metropolis Performing Arts Centre, where locals can take improv or acting classes as well as catch a show. And of course, with easy access to Chicago, fans of the performing arts are only minutes from the Chicago Theatre, the Auditorium Theatre, and the Lyric Opera House.

Like many of the top cities on this year’s U.S. News list, Bethesda offers the comforts of suburban living with access to a major city—in this case, Washington, DC. But that doesn’t mean locals have to commute for culture. Bethesda has plenty going on in terms of arts and entertainment. For music lovers, there’s the Strathmore, a 1,976-seat theater that regularly hosts the National Philharmonic Orchestra; and the Bethesda Theater, home to concerts as well as comedy shows. Meanwhile theater enthusiasts flock to Round House, and fans of the visual arts find plenty of eye candy in the city’s Arts & Entertainment District, with its galleries and public art.

Outdoor recreation is a strong attraction in Sioux Falls.

Catch the Big Sioux River cascading over pink quartzite rock at the 123-acre Falls Park; explore the world’s largest annual exhibit of public sculptures at SculptureWalk; and hit the powder at Great Bear Ski Valley—it’s all part of the lifestyle in Sioux Falls, South Dakota’s largest city. Living here also means affordable housing—with the median home cost at $315,767, compared to the national average of $370,489—plus no state income tax. The city’s low unemployment rate and excellent public safety are other reasons Sioux City landed in the top 50 on the U.S. News list. But, of course, the real draw here is the area’s natural beauty. In addition to the waterfalls mentioned above, the city is home to a 45-mile system of biking trails that connects various parks; this includes a 19-mile loop along the Big Sioux River.

Round Rock is within easy grasp of Austin but also boasts its own thriving cultural scene.

For those itching to live in Austin (ranked #164 on the U.S. News list) but not thrilled about the capital city’s high costs, Round Rock may be the place to be. Only about 30 minutes north of Austin, Round Rock has a median home value of $446,967, compared to $581,104 in the big city, according to U.S. News. But planting roots in this suburb doesn’t mean you have to totally sacrifice culture. Round Rock has a spirited arts scene, including public murals and sculptures in its downtown, as well as a brand-new creative hub called the City Arts Center. Opened in January 2026, the center is located in downtown’s historic Griffith Building, providing 44,000 square feet and two-story-high cathedral ceilings for art exhibitions, film screenings, and live music.

An aerial view of El Paso, Texas, and Juarez, Mexico

Affordable housing isn’t El Paso’s only draw, but it’s a big one. The average house costs $196,914 here, compared with a national average of $359,870. And for roughly 45% less, you get nearly 300 days of sunshine and the largest state park in an urban setting. Franklin Mountains State Park is almost 27,000 acres of desert terrain, including over 100 miles of trails for hiking and biking. Architecturally, you’ll find everything from adobe to Art Deco styles. The city’s Mission of Guadalupe dates all the way back to the 1650s, and the Socorro Mission was built in 1840. Prolific architect Henry Trost rolled into town in 1903, and he and his firm would eventually design more than 300 buildings in El Paso, adding Prairie, Spanish Colonial, Art Deco, Gothic, and Byzantine styles to the area.

For a luxury apartment in a historic high-rise, you might think you have to head to a major city, like New York or Chicago. But Appleton, about 30 miles southwest of Green Bay, offers architecturally unique apartment living. Its neo-Gothic Zuelke Building, constructed in 1931 and the city’s first high-rise, has been converted into luxury apartments, with the building’s original brass elevators and pink marble floors restored. Nearby, the Historic Fox River Mills Apartments are spread across three restored paper mills. The brick buildings, all of which are on the National Register of Historic Places, date from 1883 through 1915. And it’s not just the apartments that are appealing to design lovers—downtown Appleton is a hub for creativity. In addition to live music, the Trout Museum of Art, and the Fox Cities Performing Arts Center, the area is home to Creative Downtown Appleton, Inc., an organization that actively funds public art and urban design improvements.

Snowcapped Mount Rainier in Bellevue, Washington

Located directly across Lake Washington from Seattle, Bellevue earns high praise for its booming economy. Major corporations, including Microsoft, Amazon, T-Mobile, and Expedia Group, have offices here, and the average household income is $172,076, compared with a national average of $83,181. Of course it’s a good thing that wages run higher here, as the average home value is a staggering $1,304,230. But if you can swing the high cost, you’ll also get top-tier schools, an exceptionally safe and clean city, and extraordinary outdoor experiences. Take, for example, Bellevue Downtown Park, a 21-acre oasis in the heart of the city that features a 240-foot-wide waterfall and views of Mount Rainier in the distance.

Farmington Hills is about 20 miles northwest of downtown Detroit.

This Detroit suburb has Michigan’s largest dedicated municipal Cultural Arts Division, which coordinates year-round programs, including classes, concerts, and exhibitions. Farmington Hills is also home to The Hawk—an award-winning 270,000-square-foot recreation and arts venue that includes the Hawk Theatre, where Grammy-celebrated musicians have performed; several 2D and 3D art studios; gallery spaces that showcase local, regional, and national talent; and the Hawk Makerspace, an immersive shared creative and technical studio. The city’s Cultural Art Division also plans and juries Art on the Grand, an annual fair held in neighboring Farmington each June. The event features paintings, ceramics, and photography for sale, plus art demos and live music.

Though the median household income here is just under the national average, both the unemployment rate and average housing cost are also below the national average. In terms of cultural appeal, Oklahoma’s largest city and its capital has a number of museums, including the Oklahoma City Museum of Art and performing arts venues that host ballets, operas, and musical theater productions. Plus, OKC’s Paseo Arts District, a neighborhood just north of downtown, has 80 working artists and 20 studios that take part in an art walk the first Friday of every month, sharing their latest collections.

In the Hawkeye State, Cedar Rapids has a reputation as an artistic hub. In the 1920s and ’30s, American Regionalist painter Grant Wood, best known for his work American Gothic, lived here. Residents can enjoy his creations at various locations around town, including at the Cedar Rapids Museum of Art, home to the world’s largest collection of work by Wood; at the Veterans Memorial Building, which has a Wood-designed 24-foot-tall stained-glass window; and at the Grant Wood Studio, the artist’s former home and workspace, now owned and operated by the Cedar Rapids Museum of Art. Add to that, a number of Wood’s paintings can be found hanging in the town’s elementary and high schools, giving local kids regular access to celebrated art.

Job opportunities in tech, education, and health care abound in Austin, as do activities for the design-loving crowd. Museums in town include The Contemporary Austin, the Blanton Museum of Art, and the Mexic-Arte Museum. The last in that list is located in Austin’s bustling Warehouse District, where old warehouses have been ingeniously redesigned to host restaurants, bars, and shops. Twice a year, the arts nonprofit Big Medium coordinates studio tours, offering a peek behind the creative curtains of nearly 500 local artists and makers.

#4914. Tesla and SpaceX take first step towards merger, would dilute all shareholders

Tesla and SpaceX have both formed special committees within their corporate boards to explore the possibility of merging the two companies according to Elon Musk, who is CEO of both companies.

The merger could have big consequences not just for Tesla and SpaceX shareholders, but could dilute the retirement savings of everyone with exposure to major stock indices.

SpaceX held its quarterly earnings call today, just a few months after going public for the first time.

And for us in the electric car world, the big and unsurprising news was that Tesla and SpaceX are now formally reviewing the possibility of merging the companies together.

The possibility of a merger has been rumored for a long time. Musk has long complained of the need to respond to shareholders’ concerns as CEO of Tesla. It is odd, then, for him to take SpaceX public when he has complained for more than a decade about Tesla being public and having to respond to shareholders.

The problem, as Musk sees it, is that he does not have enough control of Tesla. Over the years, his ownership percentage had dwindled as Tesla sold stock in offerings or granted stock to employees, though today after the restoration of his illegal pay package, his ownership percentage runs around 22%.

This means he can’t ram anything through that he wants, he has to build consensus around his ideas. (That said, shareholders have proven themselves happy to oblige any ridiculous idea that he proposes to them…)

But that’s not enough for Musk. He wants total control of the company, and he’ll try any financial shenanigans to get it. He’s gone so far as to market this idea by saying that he needs $1 trillion so he can control a robot army.

If he gets that most recent pay package, a huge chunk of shares will be created out of thin air, going right into the pocket of the one person on the planet who needs them the least, and diluting the voting power and value of every other person’s shares.

So, he cooked up a plan. Sell the most ridiculous CEO pay package ever devised to Tesla shareholders, making big claims that the stock will only be delivered if Tesla manages to deliver a million robots, a million robotaxis, and various other operational milestones that would surely indicate Tesla’s success as a company.

Then do the same with SpaceX, promising to put a million colonists on Mars (which will not happen). Make sure to give yourself super-voting shares before SpaceX goes public, so you don’t have to worry about ever listening to anyone else.

Let these high-profile targets grab headlines, and trick shareholders who don’t know any better into voting for these pay packages, thinking they’re safe because even if their shares are diluted by these massive stock grants, they’ll just end up with a slightly smaller piece of a much larger pie. It’s a win-win, right?

Well… unless we include a provision in the pay package that says the shares are automatically delivered in the case of a merger. That’s right, if SpaceX and Tesla merge, then all the talk about robots and Mars colonies is irrelevant. Musk gets his stock regardless of any operational milestones.

He gets stock, you get diluted, and you didn’t even see a single robot delivered.

And so, after only the second quarterly report ever presented by SpaceX, the companies are already exploring the possibility of merging.

Musk said today during SpaceX’s earnings call that each company has formed a “special committee” of “independent board members” (and those quotes around the word “independent” are doing heavy lifting) which are reviewing the possibility of a merger.

This does not mean that the merger is a certain thing. First, the “independent” board members need to agree that it’s a good idea – but, given that Tesla’s board has always sought Musk’s interests and not those of the company, it certainly seems that if Musk thinks it’s a good idea, the committee probably will too.

After all, the special committee on pay signed off on Musk’s ridiculous trillion-dollar pay package, despite that all that package did was attach the company to the very anchor that is dragging it down. That package would benefit Musk at the cost of all other shareholders and the company’s own operations, so the board’s independence is called into question if that’s the kind of idea it signs off on.

Musk is not officially allowed to be involved in these discussions, nor are boardmembers not deemed “independent,” like his brother, Kimbal Musk. But Elon has made it clear that he wants this to happen. He did so again today, when he said that he thinks a merger would be a good idea, because “we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity” (notably, we are not, and neither would that be particularly relevant to an auto manufacturer).

So, a board sign-off seems reasonably certain given what Musk has publicly (and probably illegally) directed Tesla’s captured board to do. After that, shareholders of both companies need to approve the move.

For SpaceX this is an easy one – Musk controls more than 50% of voting shares, and therefore the company will approve of the merger. He set it up this way, and the merger would give him more money and more control, so he’s going to vote for it.

For Tesla, the vote could theoretically fail to pass. The company would need a vote of 50% of all outstanding shares, not just 50% of shareholders who turn out to cast their votes.

For this reason, Tesla has already prepared a questionable “auto-vote” procedure. This would allow shareholders to set an instruction to automatically vote all of their shares with board recommendations, no matter how bad those board recommendations are to the shareholders’ own interests.

This is a big deal for Tesla, because Tesla has a larger percentage of its shares owned by retail shareholders than most companies, and retail shareholders tend to turn out in low percentages. So this is a way to encourage more retail votes – and of course, the only option is to auto-vote with the board, not to auto-vote against it.

Further, moving the companies to Texas, where corporate law is less established and where Musk has a bought-and-paid governor/attorney general’s office in his pocket, could help remove legal barriers.

So the stage has been set, and today, the companies took the first formal step towards making this merger happen.

This wouldn’t be the first merger that Musk has tricked shareholders into.

Back in 2016, Musk went on stage to demonstrate slick-looking Tesla solar roof tiles, which would be more durable than a regular roof and generate energy along the way, meaning they’d have a lower total cost of ownership.

Those solar roof tiles never made it onto the market in any significant numbers, and Tesla eventually killed the product in August of this year.

But they served their purpose – they served to sell Tesla shareholders on the idea of purchasing SolarCity, a solar startup founded by Elon Musk’s cousins, Lyndon and Peter Rive. It also allowed billions of debt from SolarCity to be absorbed by Tesla. (Hey, that kind of sounds like when Musk bought twitter for $30 billion more than it was worth, funded it with debt, shuffled that debt into SpaceX, then IPOed to offload the debt onto the public)

And now, both Tesla and SpaceX are selling their shareholders on the idea of a merger, just a week after Musk hosted a ridiculous product demo of a product that has been delayed 11 years after it was first announced, and is now being shown off in a form that will never be legal to drive on public roads. Sounds a little familiar, doesn’t it?

All of this seems like it would only be of interest to Tesla and SpaceX shareholders, but the fact of the matter is, that means it’s of interest to all of us.

The companies are two of the largest in America by market cap, which means they are included in major stock indices. And many retirement funds thus hold exposure to Tesla, and have for years.

SpaceX is a different story, since it’s a brand-new stock. Given that it just IPOed a few months ago, it wouldn’t normally be added to indices for another year. But Musk got the rules changed so that SpaceX would be included in the Nasdaq 100 index just days after IPO, which in turn means it might already be in your retirement portfolio.

So both companies are in a lot of retirement plans, and the value of those shares will be diluted by giving a bigger share of each company to Musk if the two companies merge.

The merger [...] could dilute the retirement savings of everyone with exposure to major stock indices.

Why would that matter, since it only impacts the common people? The import thing is that the plutocratic elite like Musk be given the opportunity to enrich themselves to the maximum extent possible.

Sadly, that seems to be the version of the world that we now live in.

And thus, everyone with a retirement account would be forced to contribute money to this non-performing “performance” award for a guy whose main interest, if you read his output on the platform he treats as a full-time job, is to use his unearned wealth to impose white supremacy and do things that are, and I quote one Elon Musk on this one: “not good for America or the world.”

Oh, he’s also suing to defend nude deepfakes made without consent. Hope you like your retirement money being used for that.

We wrote last October that “Elon Musk’s $1 trillion pay day gets more ridiculous the more you look into it,” and, well, it looks like the vote wasn’t the end of it.
