#4846. The 7 Best LED Face Masks for Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

For battling blemishes and signs of aging, there are few better at-home tools.

AS SOMEONE RAISED on slasher horror movies, I was always going to gravitate towards LED face masks. But while their creepy Jason Voorhees-at-a-rave look is what initially grabbed my attention, the skincare benefits are what sold me on the products. LED face masks combine the firming power of anti-aging products, the depuffing of eye cream, the energizing boost of moisturizers, and the breakout-fighting strength of acne washes—making them one of the most versatile grooming tools out there.

LED masks use specific wavelengths of light to penetrate the skin and trigger cellular changes, according to dermatologist Dr. Hannah Kopelman, MD. This can include stimulating collagen production to reduce fine lines and support firmer skin, as well as treating acne-causing bacteria and calming inflammation to promote a clearer complexion. Some devices offer all of these benefits, while others are laser-focused (get it?) on just one or two. The key is to know what each is capable of and what service you’re looking for.

Dermatologist Dr. Brian Toy, MD, warns that the market is flooded with LED face masks that vary greatly in quality and effectiveness, so it’s best to start your search as informed as possible. To temper the confusion, I went ahead and used myself, along with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors, as guinea pigs. This way, you’ll know what works and what is merely an overpriced Halloween mask.

We gave Shark Beauty CryoGlow a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award barely a month after it was released; that’s how great this LED mask is. It offers four separate treatment options that cover anything you could possibly want out of an LED face mask. The Better Aging setting uses red and infrared light to reduce wrinkles and firm skin, while Skin Clearing mode combines blue, red, and infrared light to fight blemishes and even tone.

The Skin Sustain maintains glow with a quick mix of all three LED wavelengths, and Under-Eye Revive uses cryotherapy-inspired cooling to depuff and tighten the under-eye area. You can also use this under-eye cooling ability combined with the other treatments, which roll out in three increasing levels of chill. Each is between four and eight minutes, meaning you don’t need to dedicate much time to combat whatever issue you’re after. Under-Eye Revive, you can do up to 15 minutes if you’d like, but you only need five to be effective.

Dr. Peterson Pierre, MD, FAAD, likes that this device uses red, blue, and infrared lights so that you can get a full smorgasbord of benefits, like combating acne, fighting signs of aging, reducing inflammation, and helping regulate oil production. He also digs the cooling feature and three levels of intensity. I’ve been using my CryoGlow for months, and have seen a noticeable change in the smoothness and clearness of my skin, as well as reduced redness, using The Better Aging and Skin Clearing settings. But where I saw the most immediate results was with eye puffiness.

If I’m ever running on limited sleep or recovering from a night out, I pop the mask on, and after a few minutes of Under-Eye Revive mode, I look like I’ve actually slept. The light from this device doesn’t feel glaring when you’re wearing it, so I was able to successfully walk around and multitask during my treatments.

Plus, as someone who is generally sensitive to light, it also feels a lot less intense than other options on this list, and never inspired headaches of any kind. Not to mention, it’s easy to adjust and fits my face perfectly. I only have a few nitpicks. Given the expansive options and customizability of this mask, there is a handheld controller attached to it to help you navigate. While this makes firing up the device super easy and you don’t need to rely on an app, the controller can be a bit awkward to deal with while you’re in treatment.

You can’t put it in your pocket without accidentally changing the setting, so you have to hold it, which limits the multitasking you’re able to do. Also, the mask is bulkier than its main competition for best overall, the Dr. Dennis Gross Face Mask. But when you consider that the CryoGlow is also the cheapest full-face option on this list, it’s a fair trade-off.

Read More: Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask Review

Dr. Kopelman has been recommending this LED mask to patients for years. She likes that it is FDA-cleared and offers both red and blue light; however, what she likes most about it is that it consistently delivers results. In terms of effectiveness, it’s equal to the CryoGlow. The only reason it just missed out on the top spot is that it’s over $100 more expensive and offers fewer additional treatments, like under-eye cooling. Beyond that, I find it just as successful at battling blemishes and signs of aging as the Shark Beauty.

Plus, the treatments are shorter, and you only need to wear this for three minutes a day to see results. Unlike many other options, like the CurrentBody or FAQ 202, which are made of more flexible material you can mold to your face, this design is rigid. While that may seem like a drawback, I loved it. Of all the LED masks on this list, I found Dr. Dennis Gross to be the sturdiest, and it fit my face perfectly. It’s slim, without feeling flimsy, and doesn’t weigh down my face like other similarly sturdy masks that tend to be a bit heavier, such as the Theraface Mask.

That being said, I possess an incredibly average build and face shape, so if you fall outside of those parameters, the singular and unadaptable design of this mask might not be as perfect a fit. Unlike the CryoGlow, it’s wireless when you’re using it and can be conveniently charged with any USB-C charger. This helps when traveling, though the solid design poses some challenges if you’re tight on storage space.

Similar to the Dr. Dennis Gross mask, this device is crafted with a hard, contoured shell; however, it’s far less slim. But it trades off this added bulkiness with its vibrating ability, which soothes facial tension and boosts blood flow around the eyes, brows, and scalp. It offers red, blue, and infrared light therapy to target acne, improve skin tone, and increase collagen production.

You can choose between three- or nine-minute treatment modes, though we found the longer sessions to be more effective. Sure, this mask can feel a bit heavy or bulky on the face, but the results are legit. In fact, some effects can be seen immediately, and they only increase from there. “After the very first time I used it, my skin felt softer, and my pores looked smaller,” says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower.

“Over time, my skin tone looks more even, and my skin appears to be firmer, smoother, and less puffy.” He adds that the massaging, vibrating feature is relaxing, although it can feel ticklish or even chill-inducing at times. Since it sits close to your ears, it can also get a bit loud, especially when multitasking. Still, it’s really easy to switch between settings, turn on and off, and choose the massage style you want.

If you’re solely looking to combat puffiness, dark circles, and wrinkles, Lumin is the way to go. Sure, it looks straight out of an abandoned Lone Ranger In Space reboot, but there is no device better at rejuvenating the skin around the eyes than this mask. One tester saw noticeable improvements after days of use with this device. “I naturally have darker circles, but after consistent daily use for about a week, I saw a noticeable difference in the brightness and overall alertness of my eye area,” she says. The mask stays in place well, and the soft silicone padding makes it comfortable throughout each session.

Its adjustable design also ensures it fits all face shapes and sizes with ease. The same tester also saw a brighter tone and smoother skin after a couple of weeks of daily use. “While I don’t personally have under-eye wrinkles, I can see how this would be especially helpful for someone who does or for anyone who spends a lot of time in the sun,” she says. Not to mention, the Luminator is quick and easy to use—just three minutes a day with an auto timer.

Our testers found that this FAQ mask makes a strong impression right out of the box with its ultra-thin, flexible design, which feels more like a high-end sheet mask than a tech device. You’ll need to download the app to get the most out of this tool, however. There’s a single button on the mask, but without the app, we found that it was nearly impossible to remember its function or how to power it off.

Once the app is set up and the mask is synced, navigating the features becomes straightforward—just select your desired treatment and that’s it. Despite being covered in tiny LED lights, the mask feels surprisingly lightweight and comfortable. During the 15-minute session, testers reported no heat or noticeable sensation on the skin and even forgot it was on while doing other tasks, such as reading. The mask stays comfortably in place, even when looking down at a book or phone.

We also appreciated the included cleaning spray. For anyone with sensitive or breakout-prone skin, keeping the mask clean is essential, and the spray makes that simple. After each use, we cleaned and dried the mask before placing it in its pouch, which securely holds the device and makes storage hassle-free. One minor concern was the split at the bridge of the nose—designed for flexibility—which left one tester wondering if that area was receiving full treatment. Still, this didn’t deter them from continuing to use it.

Women’s Health fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says that the Qure Pro LED Mask has taken her nightly skincare regimen to the next level. After a month of use, she saw a dramatic difference in her skin’s appearance. She used to struggle with oily skin and frequent breakouts, but since regularly using the pink LED light setting, she says it has significantly reduced her sebum production. “I'm also approaching 30 (yikes), so I've been using the red LED light setting as well to help combat fine lines and reverse skin aging,” Accardi says.

Each session runs for three minutes and automatically shuts off when it’s done, so you never have to worry about timing it yourself. It’s perfect for anyone who wants results without the hassle. It’s one of the easiest, most low-maintenance skincare tools out there at a relatively low cost. That’s not to say $380 is cheap, but when it comes to legit, effective LED masks, you won’t find many other options under $400. It’s really just this and the CryoGlow.

If the more rigid masks, like CryoGlow, Qure, and Dr. Dennis Gross, are too bulky for you, but the FAQ is too small for your face, Currentbody will be your best option. This mask offers the most flexibility, with a silicone design that easily molds to the contours of any face, ensuring full coverage. This is as long as you tighten the straps. I’ve been lazy a few times with that, and it will start slipping off your face mid-treatment. In addition to the flexible fit, this mask feels super gentle on the face.

One of our testers used it only days after getting eye surgery with no issue. Didn’t bother her eyes one bit. That being said, it takes up to six hours for a full charge, which can be a bit annoying. This is the longest charge time on this list by a few hours, to be clear. I’m the type of person who pushes off charging a device until I absolutely have to, so this long charge time usually results in me skipping a day of treatment. But if you’re a better planner (to be fair, it’s a low bar compared to me), it’ll be less of an issue.

Depending on what skin issues or concerns you’re looking to address with your LED face mask, you’ll want to focus on which treatments it offers. This is driven by the color of light the device uses, which dictates its benefits. Some on this list offer multiple services, while others zero in on one. These are the common options:

While some are comfortable and allow for multitasking, there is no getting around the fact that you’re wearing a large light on your face. As a long-time migraine sufferer, having a light this close to my eyes for too long can be a trigger. But even if you’re perfectly fine with prolonged light exposure, you’ll want to know what the time commitment is before buying LED face masks, as they’re most effective when used regularly. Some are as long as 25 minutes, while others can be as short as three minutes. Keep in mind that not all are meant for everyday use; some (especially the ones with longer treatment lengths) may only need to be used a few times a week for max efficiency.

When shopping for an LED face mask, choosing a device that’s FDA-cleared is essential, says Dr. Kopelman. This ensures the product meets fundamental safety standards for consumer use. To be clear, however, FDA-cleared is not the same as FDA-approved—the latter involves extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing. Currently, no LED face masks on the market have achieved FDA approval.

For now, stick with FDA-cleared options, which means the device is proven to be as safe and effective as another legally marketed product. You might also see terms like FDA-registered or FDA-listed, but these simply indicate that the manufacturer has notified the FDA of the product's existence—there’s no review or evaluation involved. Because of that uncertainty, you won’t see any of those on this list.

There are a lot of LED face masks out there, and like any trendy tool, not all are created equal. So, before putting any to the test, I consulted with a panel of dermatologists on which devices were legit and which they recommend. They also advised me on what to look for in a quality LED face mask and the brands to focus on. Based on this intel, I, along with other Men’s Health writers and editors, put several masks to the test, evaluating each device’s effectiveness, ease of use, and how comfortable it was to wear.

As many LED face masks do not offer immediate results, we used each one for at least one month to ensure enough time was given to gain any possible benefits. Following this extensive research and testing, I landed on these seven LED face masks as the best for men in 2026.

The dermatologists I spoke to for this story were clear on this: you should be cleaning your device after every use. If you don’t, bacteria, oil, and product residue can build up on the surface and transfer back onto your skin, causing irritation or breakouts, which may ironically be what you were hoping to minimize by using an LED mask in the first place.

Dr. Kopelman says that LED masks should always be used on freshly cleansed, dry skin to ensure the light penetrates as effectively as possible. After the session, apply your serums and moisturizers—doing it beforehand can block the light and reduce its benefits. A hydrating serum like hyaluronic acid or a peptide-rich cream works especially well to complement the collagen boost from the treatment, Dr. Kopelman says.

According to Dr. Toy, be sure to skip any products that might react to light. For example, because retinol and vitamin C serums are photosensitizing, they’re an absolute no-go before any LED treatment. Dr. Chacon adds that reflective products like heavy oils or sunscreens should also be avoided during use as they can scatter the light and disrupt the device’s effectiveness.

#4845. Melatonin Is Not Just for Sleep

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Melatonin is widely known as the substance that makes us sleepy. It is commonly used as an over-the-counter sleep aid to treat jet lag and bouts of insomnia. However, new research shows that melatonin plays a wider role in maintaining overall health. Melatonin is a potent antioxidant that can prevent tissue damage. Evidence suggests it could help ward off certain types of cancer (Proietti, Reiter & Bizzarriet, 2012). It plays an essential role in the immune system’s ability to fight infections and heal from injuries (Szataniak & Packi, 2025; Singh et al., 2024).

Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is known as a chronobiotic hormone, which means that it regulates circadian rhythm. Tryptophan, an amino acid ingested from certain foods, serves as a building block for the production of serotonin. Serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation, is converted to melatonin primarily in the brain’s pineal gland. Production of melatonin is increased during darkness at night and it is released directly into the bloodstream. Levels decline during the day as production is inhibited by light (Kamfar et al., 2024).

Sleep has long been known to promote healing. People need extra sleep to recover from physical ailments. Research published in 2025 by Szataniak et al. showed that immune responses are strongly affected by the sleep cycle. The authors analysed 59 studies published from 2000-2025 that examined how melatonin production affects the immune system. They found that chronic sleep deprivation impairs immune response which increases susceptibility to infections and inflammation (Szataniak, et al 2025).

Pro-inflammatory molecules of the immune system, called cytokines, mobilize aggressive responses to fight off viruses, infections or foreign pathogens. This process is most active during sleep. Elevated levels of cytokines during infections or inflammation promote increased sleepiness associated with illness. This is an adaptive response and serves to promote recovery (Singh et al., 2024).

In 2024, Singh et al. published results that showed decreased melatonin levels correlate with increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines. They found that chronic sleep deprivation increases cytokine production, contributing to systemic low-grade inflammation. This imbalance potentially increases the risk for cardiovascular disease, cancer, atherosclerosis, diabetes, and autoimmune illnesses (Szataniak et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2024). Chronic elevation of these cytokines has also been found to be associated with fatigue and immunosuppression (Szataniak et al., 2025).

Another component of the immune response acts to quiet the system and heal from inflammation and infections. Anti-inflammatory molecules such as the hormone cortisol are enhanced during wakefulness and play an essential role in regulating sleep and immune function (Singh et al., 2024). Cortisol reduces inflammation in the body and has immunosuppressant effects. It increases the sense of alertness, and like melatonin it is released following a circadian rhythm (Hoyt, Zeiders, Ehrlich & Adam, 2016). Levels of cortisol are highest early in the morning and decrease throughout the day. During sleep, cortisol levels are decreased while melatonin levels are increased. Chronic sleep deprivation can disrupt cortisol secretion, leading to a negative impact on immunity and susceptibility to infections (Singh et al., 2024).

Getting enough sleep is essential for maintaining physical health. Screening for insomnia should be included in routine healthcare visits. Education and increased awareness regarding the importance of adequate sleep should be part of health and wellness initiatives (Szataniak et al., 2025). Recently, enhanced widespread screening for pain issues and depression have been incorporated into medical visits. This should be expanded to include regular sleep assessments.

Evidence supports the use of dietary supplements containing melatonin or its precursor tryptophan to treat certain types of short-term sleep disruption (Szataniak et al., 2025; American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2021). However, melatonin supplementation is not recommended as a long-term strategy for treatment of chronic insomnia (AASM, 2021). The American Academy of Sleep Medicine emphasizes the importance of assessing underlying causes of insomnia. They recommend implementing behavioral routines to improve sleep. Collectively referred to as sleep hygiene, this includes strategies such as turning off electronic devices (for example phones, television, and computers) 30 to 60 minutes before bed, adhering to a consistent sleep schedule, and caution around substances such as caffeine and alcohol.

About 10% of adults meet criteria for chronic insomnia disorder (AASM, 2021). In these cases, a course of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia or CBT-I is recommended. Medications for insomnia are generally considered a last resort after behavioral options have been implemented (AASM, 2021).

More recent research presented at the 2025 American Heart Association conference examined long-term melatonin use in 130,828 adults diagnosed with insomnia. Results showed that the use of melatonin for 12 months or more was correlated with an increased likelihood of being diagnosed with heart failure or dying from any cause over the course of five years. Although cause and effect was not proven, it highlights potential cardiovascular risks and the need for further research to establish the safety of long-term melatonin use (American Heart Association, 2025).

Hormones, including melatonin, are part of a complex endocrine system that exert multiple effects on different organs. Maintaining balance promotes resilience and wellness. Adequate sleep is a critical component to maintaining long-term health and optimal immune function. (Singh et al., 2024).

#4844. Kia’s EV6 GT beat out the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 in a German EV comparison test

Kia’s electric sports car beat out the Tesla Model Y Performance and BYD’s Sealion 7 in a recent comparison test by the German magazine Auto Motor und Sport, ranking first overall.

It wasn’t a German brand or a Chinese one. It wasn’t even the Tesla Model Y Performance. Kia’s electric sports car, the EV6 GT, took first place in a recent high-performance EV test in Germany, the heart of Europe.

The comparison test, held by German auto magazine Auto Motor und Sport, evaluated five high-performance EVs across seven categories: body, safety, comfort and convenience, powertrain, driving performance, environmental friendliness, and running costs.

The EV6 GT ranked first overall with 585 points, 9 points ahead of the Tesla Model Y Performance, which took second with 576 points.

The Zeekr 7GT ranked third with 569 points, followed by the Polestar 4 Coupe Dual Motor with 531 points, and the BYD Sealion 7 AWD Excellence, which ranked fifth with 508 points.

Kia’s electric sports car took the top spot in three of the seven categories: safety, powertrain, and driving performance. In the safety category, the EV6 GT scored highest for its superior braking and high-speed stability.

The EV6 GT earned praise in the powertrain category, boasting up to 650 horsepower and 770 Nm of torque from its dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain.

In the driving performance category, Kia’s electric sports car scored 20 points higher (96 points) than the Tesla Model Y Performance in second (76 points).

According to Auto Motor und Sport, the Kia EV6 GT took first place overall in the comparison test due to its “outstanding driving performance.”

Performance is one thing, but it also stands out with fun features, including Virtual Gear Shift. Borrowed from the Hyundai IONIQ 5 N, the feature simulates the feeling and sounds of a six-speed paddle-operated transmission.

Kia overhauled the interior for the newest model with its new connected car Navigation Cockpit (ccNC) infotainment system.

The new system includes dual 12.3″ navigation and driver display screens in a curved panoramic setup.

Kia’s electric sports car can sprint from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds. It uses a new 84 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

With 800V fast-charging capabilities, the Kia EV6 GT can recharge from 10% to 80% in as little as 18 minutes.

In Germany, the new Kia EV6 GT starts at 69,990 euros ($78,000). The Tesla Model Y Performance, on the other hand, starts at 63,970 euros in Germany. It offers a WLTP range of up to 360 miles (580 km) and accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds.

Which high-performance EV would you drive? The Kia EV6 GT or the Tesla Model Y Performance? Let us know in the comments.

Unfortunately, Kia said it was discontinuing the EV6 GT in the US “until further notice” earlier this year.

The right oil fixes everything, like itch, frizz, and dryness. These are the ones worth your time.

THERE ARE PLENTY of reasons to grow a beard—extra protection from the sun and cold, having something to caress when thinking, or, in my case, faking a sharper jawline. But for most guys, the biggest motivator is convenience. A beard may be easier than daily shaving, but it still needs attention. You have to learn how to trim it, shape it, and use the right beard products to keep it looking good. And no product pulls more weight than a quality beard oil.

Facial hair is naturally coarser and drier, and without proper care, it can feel itchy, scraggly, and uncomfortable. That’s where beard oil comes in. It acts like a conditioner tailored for your face, softening the hair while keeping the skin underneath hydrated and healthy. Dudes with big, full beards may struggle to work a thick balm through all that hair, making a lightweight oil the easier, more effective option.

But beard oils aren’t just for lumberjack-level growth. They help moisturize, reduce itch, and protect any style, from stubble to a full mane. The short version: When your skin and hair stay hydrated, everything looks and feels better.

This beard oil offers the most wide-ranging benefits of any I’ve tested. It hydrates, softens, soothes, exfoliates, and even keeps my beard smelling clean, which is exactly why we gave it a Men’s Health Smell Fresh Award last year. The lightweight blend of argan, rice bran, and apple seed oils smooths out scruff while keeping the skin underneath hydrated, and the papaya and lavender oils gently buff away flakes and calm irritation without leaving any greasy shine behind.

The rosemary-powered deodorizing complex is also a game-changer, neutralizing odor so my mustache and beard stay fresh from morning to night. And because it works on everything—from stubble to a full, dense beard—it’s one of the most versatile grooming products I’ve added to my routine. Clean, subtle in scent, and ridiculously effective, it’s the definition of a multitasker. The beard oil version of a walking desk.

Read More: 2026 Men's Health Smell Fresh Awards

What grabbed me right away about this beard oil is how much hydration you get from such a clean, simple formula. It’s packed with the heavy hitters—jojoba, argan, avocado, grapeseed—basically a greatest-hits lineup for soft, healthy whiskers. Even though it’s marketed toward guys with thick, rough beards, I found it surprisingly lightweight and easy to use on shorter growth, too.

Because the oil absorbs so well, I only need a drop or two to keep longer or bushier beards smooth for hours. And if you’re prone to breakouts, relax: the formula is non-comedogenic, so it won’t clog your pores or leave your skin angry. It’s also a no-brainer for anyone who avoids fragrance.

While this stuff isn’t completely unscented, the fragrance is as minimal as it gets. I have sensitive skin and saw no irritation, as well as no cologne cloud living under my nose all day. If you prefer your beard oil to work without announcing itself, this one’s ideal.

This beard oil has the richest texture of all I’ve tried, thanks to its avocado-oil base. Long beards burn through moisture quickly, and this formula actually keeps up, sinking in deep to soften and smooth without leaving a heavy, greasy layer behind. Squalane—one of my favorite skincare ingredients—lightens the blend just enough so my beard feels conditioned and controlled instead of weighed down.

You also get the skin benefits of vitamin E, which helps calm irritation under the beard and keeps everything feeling comfortable throughout the day. The scent is low-key but luxe: a mix of cedarwood, jasmine, and sandalwood that feels warm and spa-like before disappearing into the background. And despite the small bottle, a few drops are all you need, even if your beard’s edging into Gandalf territory.

I know I said never to buy a beard oil for the scent, but this option is an exception. With a rich palo santo fragrance that also blends in bright cardamom and dry papyrus, this beard oil makes my beard smell clean, smooth, and surprisingly refined. It keeps that freshness going all day, no matter how long my beard gets.

The formula does serious work too: on shorter growth, it calms irritation and helps keep ingrowns from flaring up, and on longer beards, it replaces the moisture facial hair naturally loses, softening dry ends and hydrating the skin underneath. A few drops give me a conditioned, healthy-looking beard that smells incredible without ever overpowering my face.

Hair oil is the most underrated styling product for men, as it hydrates and shields strands to create a smoother base that helps other products apply better and work more effectively. I’ve also found that it’s the easiest to forget. When I’ve recently put my brain cells through the wringer and face a subsequent rise in forgetfulness, a dual-purpose beard and hair oil is my savior—and none are better than Aesop’s

No matter how out of it I may be, I always remember to apply my beard oil (my face is way too itchy without it), so the bottle serves as a nice reminder to run my hands through my head as well. Barely half a vial full is enough to cover both my beard and hair, leaving both feeling softer and more hydrated. Plus, this is Aesop, so the scent is incredible. It has an earthy, bright fragrance that continues Aesop’s trend of being the only brand to pull off essential oil/incense-type scents.

I have a slew of skin and scalp issues, but one area in grooming I’ve never struggled with is growing hair (he said, knocking profusely on wood). Still, when I’m in the early stages of growing a beard, it’s nice to have a boost. That’s where Asna’s aptly named Beard Boost Oil comes in. It’s loaded with vitamins A, C, E, and B to support healthier and stronger strands, while squalane deeply hydrates and smooths the hair shaft. Together, they reduce dryness and frizz so your beard appears denser, softer, and fuller.

To be clear, it won’t necessarily help your beard grow, but it will help it appear thicker, which is the next best thing. The sandalwood scent is subtle and pleasant, so I never have to worry about it clashing with stronger fragrances. This oil is also the thickest on this list, which takes some getting used to. However, once you do, it’s a positive because you only need to use a couple of drops to cover your beard.

All but one beard oil on this list comes in one-ounce bottles (Aesop is 0.8 ounces), which makes it even more impressive that Horace’s lasts noticeably longer. The dropper dispenses tiny amounts at a time, preventing overuse, and the lightweight formula spreads easily—I only need two to three drops, depending on my beard length.

It’s also the best pick for guys who prefer a fresher scent. While most beard oils lean woody or earthy, Horace stands out with a subtle lemon-and-mint blend that won’t clash with amber or wood-forward colognes but still feels like a clean break from the usual.

If you’re anything like me, you drink roughly two pots of coffee a day. Just the smell of it gives me a burst of energy, which is what I love about this beard oil’s caffeinated scent. After a rough night or ahead of a busy day when I’ll need as much energy as I can get, getting whiffs of this beard oil gives me an added boost—or at least helps remind me to have another cup.

I also have a love of brown liquor that was likely preordained by my Irish heritage, so the hint of whisky scent in this oil is welcomed, though the smell of coffee is stronger. This is probably a good thing; I don’t need a reminder to have another one of those. Performance-wise, Viking Revolution is as effective as you can find under $10.

Its 100 percent argan and jojoba oils blend keeps whiskers feeling soft for hours. That being said, I do find I need to use a little bit more of this stuff to cover my entire beard than other options on this list. But for the price point and scent, it’s well worth it.

What really makes or breaks a beard oil is the blend of oils inside. You want ingredients that actually penetrate the hair and nourish the skin—not heavy oils that sit on top and leave your beard feeling slick and suffocated. Look for lightweight, fast-absorbing oils like jojoba, argan, grapeseed, avocado, and castor, which sink in quickly without leaving a greasy film. These not only soften your whiskers but also keep the skin beneath your beard healthy and hydrated.

Because beard oil is massaged from the roots to the ends, anything too thick can clog pores underneath, leading to irritation or those deep, painful beard pimples every guy dreads. Smart formulas use blends of light oils—often combined with extras like marula, sweet almond, squalane, or vitamin E—to boost moisture, strengthen hair, and calm inflamed skin without weighing things down. As long as the base oils are lightweight and absorbent, a multi-oil mix is exactly what you want.

Fragrance shouldn’t be the main reason you reach for a beard oil, especially if you have sensitive skin, but it can be a great bonus. Plenty of beard oils have masculine, cologne-quality scents that give the product some added value. Plus, it’ll give you something pleasant to smell on your mustache all day.

That being said, strong scents can easily trigger irritation, so stick to oils with a subtle aroma that comes naturally from the ingredients themselves. Added fragrances are common irritants, and even high concentrations of essential oils can cause redness or flare-ups.

If you’re not sure how your skin will react, do a quick patch test. Apply a small amount to one spot, then wait a few hours (or even overnight). No redness, itching, or bumps? You’re in the clear and good to use it everywhere.

I’ve had a beard for so long that I barely remember my face without one, which means I’ve spent the better part of two decades testing every type of beard product out there, including more oils than I can count. Over the past two years, I’ve compared notes with fellow Men’s Health editors, swapped favorites, and put a fresh batch of formulas through daily testing to see which ones actually deliver softer, healthier, better-looking whiskers.

With all that experience, I was able to narrow the field before spending months trying different oils on everything from short stubble to full-grown scruff. I looked at how well they hydrated, how fast they absorbed, how they felt on the skin underneath, and whether they left any greasy residue behind. Price, scent, and ingredient quality all factored in, too. What you’ll find below are my honest picks for the best beard oils worth buying in 2026, options that truly elevate your grooming routine, whether you’re rocking light stubble or a full-on mane.

For the best results, I like to treat my beard the same way I treat the hair on my head: regular washing and consistent conditioning. Clean it a few times a week with a beard-specific wash to remove buildup, then follow with a good beard oil. Before applying the oil, smooth out your beard with a comb, brush, or even your fingers so you’re starting with the shape you want.

Warm a small amount of oil between your palms and work in from the cheeks and chin, massaging it in the same way you’d apply a face moisturizer. Make sure you’re getting all the way down to the skin—that’s what keeps dryness, itch, and irritation away. If your beard is longer, finish by running your fingers through the length in downward strokes to coat every strand.

#4842. What We Really Talk About When We Talk About Frivolous Things

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

There’s a scene in the 1996 film Trainspotting, based on the Irvine Welsh novel, and recently resurrected in London’s West End, where the boys ask the girls what they’re talking about, and the girls say, “Shopping!” Their throwaway response is shorthand for “frivolous girly things.” I enjoy conversations, with female friends and Gen Z clients alike, about “frivolous girly things”, except, in therapy, as in Trainspotting, we’re often talking about something deeper as well.

In my early career I had an 18-year-old client called Polly*. She was attractive and always immaculately made-up and fashionably dressed, with fantastic hair. She loved shopping for clothes and would often tell me about her latest buys. Most weeks, Polly complimented something about my appearance:

Polly was socially polite, compliant and genial. I liked her, and I liked talking with her about clothes and hair and make-up. We also talked about Polly’s strong need to be “likeable” and her self-identification as a “people pleaser”. She was exceptionally observant, hypervigilant at times, and we explored the ways this linked to her history of trauma.

But Polly noticed me too. With the benefit of hindsight (and experience), I understand Polly’s compliments as communicating something about our relationship that I’d missed an opportunity to explore. She noticed that I bothered to tidy up my hair and think about my clothes before I met with her, which demonstrated that I thought she was worth making the effort for. Her comments could therefore be interpreted as gratitude: “Thanks for caring.” I knew from the stories she shared that not everyone paid her the same level of respect, which was demonstrated in the ways they presented themselves when they met her.

Polly talked about the time she met her mother for coffee. Her mother, was shabbily clad in a tracksuit and trainers but had a dress and sandals in her bag to change into before she went on to lunch with “the girls”. The underlying message was: “You’re not important enough to make an effort for.”

Polly mentioned a tutor who showed her the jacket she’d purchased at lunchtime and quipped that it was much too nice to wear in college. In other words, “It’s much too nice to wear here, with you.”

And I’d heard about the boyfriend who refused to dress up for date nights but had no qualms about doing so for drinks with the boys. The unconscious communication was, “I’m bothered about them more than I’m bothered about you.”

Appearances mattered to Polly; it was a way to express herself and one of the few things she could control. But her compliments about my appearance communicated the importance of what it symbolised about our relationship too. The clues were there all along in what Polly shared with me about her other significant relationships, but I didn’t notice at the time.

So, when Polly complimented how I looked, it wasn’t about me, it was about us. Her unconscious communication was: “I’ve noticed you care about me and our relationship and I’m grateful.” I’ve learnt to be more curious about compliments and ever mindful of the subtleties of both my verbal responses and involuntary facial expressions. These are the unconscious communications that pass between my clients and me when we talk about frivolous girly things.

* Polly, her mother, her tutor and her boyfriend are fictitious composites.

#4841. Increasing Ozempic Dose Linked to Lower Heart Risk Than Switching to Mounjaro

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

Increasing the dose of Ozempic rather than switching to Mounjaro may be associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), according to a 2026 insurance claims analysis presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting 2026 in Milan, Italy.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) have reshaped care for people with type 2 diabetes, but recent real-world evidence suggests these drugs may not offer identical heart protection.

It is important to keep in mind that this was a retrospective, observational study that showed an association, not causation.

More research is needed to fully compare the cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide versus tirzepatide.

The COMPETE SWITCH Cardiovascular (CV) analysis used Komodo Health’s Healthcare Map, a large US healthcare claims database with linked laboratory results, to examine real-world data from 636,525 adults with type 2 diabetes.

The analysis focused on 185,705 people who increased their semaglutide dose and 23,104 who switched to tirzepatide.

All participants included in the analysis were already receiving 1 mg of semaglutide (Ozempic) weekly.

The researchers found that people who increased their Ozempic dose to 2 mg had a 6% lower risk of MACE — including all-cause death, myocardial infarction (heart attack), and stroke — compared with those who switched to Mounjaro at doses up to 15 mg.

“This is an interesting study, but the findings may partly reflect medication adherence. When patients switch medications, it can take time to adjust the dose and find the right treatment level, which may temporarily affect how well their condition is controlled,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

He also noted that the study did not determine what might explain the difference in cardiovascular risk.

“It may be related to a combination of weight loss and direct effects on hormones involved in metabolism and appetite regulation,” Ali said.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both GLP-1 medications. Ozempic (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are approved to help manage type 2 diabetes, while each medication also has a different brand approved for weight loss.

The semaglutide approved for weight loss in the U.S. is sold as Wegovy, and the tirzepatide approved for weight loss is sold as Zepbound.

“Semaglutide and tirzepatide work in a similar way. While semaglutide is a direct GLP-1 receptor agonist, tirzepatide is a dual agonist of both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors,” Amit Blumfield, MD, with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

“Because they work through somewhat different pathways, they can have different effects in individual patients,” added Ali.

While both semaglutide (Ozemipc) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) work in similar ways, you may find that you tolerate one better than the other.

Ali noted that you should discuss any potential benefits and drawbacks with your healthcare professional.

“I would only recommend switching medications if there is an issue with tolerance of one or the other. If one medication is well-tolerated at increasingly higher doses and is effective in the desired weight-loss and blood sugar management, I wouldn’t necessarily switch,” added Blumfield.

These side effects are generally mild and may lessen over time. However, if side effects become difficult to tolerate, you should speak with your healthcare professional.

“GLP-1 medications can be highly effective for managing diabetes and promoting weight loss, but there is no one-size-fits-all treatment. The best medication depends on an individual’s health needs, goals, response to treatment, and potential side effects,” said Ali.

#4840. A Reader’s Guide to the Many Sexy Roles of Alexander Skarsgård

Hollywood initially tried to make the 50-year-old star into a traditional hunk. He got weirder—and hotter—instead.

FAR TOO OFTEN, today’s Hollywood hunks deny their beauty to play a cavalcade of schmucks, freaks, and losers with funny accents, hiding in prosthetics because they think this will transform them into “serious” actors in the public eye. But this strategy doesn’t always pay off. Leo spent two hours and 42 minutes running around in a plaid bathrobe and messy man bun only to lose the Best Actor Oscar to Michael B. Jordan, who played a smokeshow vampire with a spit kink (and his identically sexy twin).

It’s best not to underestimate someone with undeniable sex appeal and unquenchable blood lust, as Alexander Skarsgård knows all too well from his years playing Eric Northman on True Blood. The role not only made Stockholm’s native son a household name in America, but an instantly recognizable sex symbol. Not that he needed much help from Hollywood. Skarsgård is 6'4" of muscle with anime bone structure. He’s 50, but doesn’t age in human years. He makes us mere mortal men all look, and feel, lesser than. The scion of Swedish acting royalty comes from a place where everyone kind of looks like that, yet he’s been named Sweden’s Sexiest Man Alive five times.

“After my first job, I was on a stupid ‘sexy hunky hot list’ and then people didn’t take me seriously,” Skarsgård told the The Sunday Times in 2022. “If you want characters with depth but have been labelled ‘a dude who takes his shirt off’, you’re not going to get those offers.” At the time, he was promoting The Northman, for which he’d packed on 25 additional pounds of muscle to play a Viking warrior prince, and spent most of his screen time shirtless, delivering the exact sort of performance that theoretically typecast him in the first place.

From scanning his filmography, it’s clear that at a certain point, Skarsgård decided to lean into his lot in life as an unapologetic sex symbol. Over the past two decades, he’s slowly gravitated toward roles that don’t attempt to soften or normalize his hunkiness, portraying a diverse range of characters who all just happen to be ridiculously hot in films and television shows that play with his beauty, what it means, and how it messes with the rest of us.

In his latest, Wicker, Skarsgård plays a literal object of desire, the purest distillation of his on-screen persona as a sweet and (still, somehow) sexy magical dildo who loves doing chores and adores his fishmonger wife (Olivia Colman), causing hysteria in a village full of dumbasses who have no idea how to treat or fuck a woman. In other words, he’s Alexander Skarsgård.

The Male Model: Zoolander & Zoolander 2 (2001 & 2016)

Ben Stiller’s comedy classic is built around the premise that Jerry Stiller’s son and Owen Wilson and Benedict Cumberbatch are male models. A fun piece of trivia is Skarsgård was inserted as one of Derek’s United Nations of conventionally attractive roommates. Baby faced Meekus is hilariously bad at bitchy teenage girl humor and loves orange mocha frappuccinos. He gets in a gasoline fight in the first installment that results in a fiery death, but returns for the sequel in a brief cameo, perfectly cast as the original man.

Skarsgård became a star when this show was a very good gothic soap opera people held in the same regard as many of the HBO classics that were on at the time, but it has faded from memory due to completely spinning off its axis in later seasons. But his role as Eric Northman, a sexy, menacing Viking prince who carries himself with regal arrogance when he first washes up in Louisiana, remains an indelible performance. He’s a kind of Magneto/Lestat figure, who believes in vampire superiority and humans primarily as food, then slowly reforms.

This remake of the 1971 Sam Peckinpah classic is a bad, hamfisted W. Bush era culture war movie (released three years late), in which James Marsden, as a pretentious, Harvard-educated lib Hollywood screenwriter, is pitted against Skarsgård, who plays a God-, guns-, country music and football-loving redneck. But the use of Skarsgård is symbolically correct: As a rugged man’s man who works with his hands, hulks over Marsden’s effete snob, and represents all Marsden’s shortcomings and insecurities.

The Charismatic Cult Leader: The East (2013) & The Stand (2020)

Two roles that trade on Skarsgård’s magnetism, casting him as cult leaders. One is Benji, an eco-terrorist ringleader in The East, which was overshadowed by Kelly Reichardt’s superior eco-terrorist anti-thriller Night Moves from the same year, but is also very good. Skarsgård begins the film as a hirsute, politically radical Jim Morrison. The role generally strips a lot of his raw tools away but he proves he still has the juice, running his operations with the certitude of a self-righteous zealot, taking full advantage of his implicit understanding that everyone will do what he says because they all want to fuck him.

That same energy is twisted evil in the less-than-stellar and largely forgotten Paramount+-produced adaptation of Stephen King’s The Stand from 2020. Skarsgård is having a blast here, clearly tapped in and comfortable with the cheap, fatty, made for TV vibes. He plays Randall Flagg, an infamous demonic anti-Christ figure in King lore, who also swaggers around making dark, grand pronouncements because he knows everyone is dreaming about him…and wants to fuck him.

The Mythological Figure: The Legend of Tarzan (2016) & The Northman (2022)

These are the two loin cloth roles that make best use of Skarsgård as physical clay. The first was a bid for a franchise at a more conventional phase of Skarsgard’s career. It’s a horribly problematic text about a Lawrence of Arabia raised by gorillas in the Congo, released at what was probably the latest moment in modern history anyone could’ve possibly thought this IP could still work in any context. And yet, Christoph Waltz is the bad guy, Margot Robbie is Jane, Samuel L. Jackson turns in a peak performance. It doesn’t really matter, because the movie doesn’t work. The one very funny, deeply horny beat, however, is Tarzan and Jane’s meet cute, when Robbie happens upon a still uncivilized, dirt and grime covered Skarsgård in the jungle, who emerges from the brush, towers over her, then sniffs her from head to toe, which is a shameless, incredibly erotic romantasy/soft porn scenario.

The Northman on the other hand, rules, and might just be the best movie in director Robert Eggers’s burgeoning and impressive filmography. I still wonder to this day how it wasn’t a bigger deal (likely the mid 2022 Covid-era release date, but still). Skarsgård leaves it all on screen in this folklore epic, near naked in the snow, in the mud, in the waves, shredded and extremely believable as a raider scaling ramparts with a battle axe, lurching through villages as they’re pillaged and burned.

The Alpha Scumbag: Big Little Lies (2017-2019)

“Biggest scumbag Alexander Skarsgård has ever played” is quite a distinction, but it has to be Perry Wright, a manipulative, abusive, domineering, womanizing monster who entwines magnetic, toxic sex with serial spousal abuse in David E. Kelly’s Shakespearean, rich, white wine-momsploitation thriller. He plays one of the few believable on-screen partners Nicole Kidman has ever had, arm candy who wears the fuck out of tailored suits. He’s a striking contrast to the show’s other husbands, all older boring, brunette, beta boys. He’s a perfect-from-a-distance husband and father, the on-paper exemplar of a certain anachronistic masculinity, and also the epitome of damaged male evil. Which is why Perry’s Orient Express style group murder is the climax of the first season of the show.

The Tech Demigod (The Odin of Codin): Succession (2018-2023)

A highly unlikely proposition. Harry Melling (who most probably still know best from his role as Dudley Dursley in the Harry Potter films) is Colin, a nebbishy mama’s boy with an aptitude for devotion in a barbershop quartet. Colin’s meetcute is delivering a back alley blowjob with little preamble to Skarsgård’s Ray, the hung final boss of leather daddies in the sweetest BDSM rom-com since Secretary. As Ray, Skarsgård communicates almost entirely via squinting, grunting, monosyllabic responses, and direct commands, yet is a completely alluring masculine ideal. His hobbies are waxing his motorcycle, watching shit on his phone while he eats, wrestling in assless unitards as foreplay, and reading Knausgaard. You can smell the sandalwood, cedar and tobacco wafting off the screen.

In which Skarsgård finally, inevitably plays a robot. This is a darkly comedic, but also occasionally saccharine, Apple TV+ series about a Wall-E war machine. His character, known only as Murderbot, has found a way to disable the guardrails that would otherwise force him to obey protocols programmed by the nefarious Weyland-Yutani style corporation who created him, and uses this freedom to consume our garbage TV shows. Murderbot expresses a professed disinterest in humanity, and hates eye contact; It’s a weird, flat, funny performance that ultimately lands halfway between Pedro Pascal in The Mandalorian and Peter Weller in Robocop. Skarsgård is a completely believable robot in a show that also serves as a metaphor for autism.

#4839. Oral GLP-1 Orforglipron (Foundayo) Achieves Weight Loss for Women of All Ages

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

A new GLP-1 pill called orforglipron (Foundayo) has been shown to help women lose weight, regardless of menopausal status, according to new research.

A group of researchers, including senior author Hunter Thomas Hoffman, PharmD, a clinical research scientist affiliated with the drug’s manufacturer, Eli Lilly, analyzed data from two prior trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, to arrive at this conclusion.

These studies reveal that this medication works equally well for women who have not yet gone through menopause, those who are currently experiencing it, and those who are postmenopausal.

The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), held in Milan, Italy, from September 28 to October 2.

This is important because menopause often causes weight gain due to lower estrogen levels, making weight loss more difficult for many women.

Orforglipron offers a promising new option for managing weight in women with obesity or overweight, especially those with type 2 diabetes.

In April of this year, Eli Lilly’s Foundayo received FDA approval as a weight-loss drug, making it the second GLP-1 pill for weight loss to enter the U.S. market after Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy.

The ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies involved women who were either obese or overweight and who had at least one medical condition related to their weight.

Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, and overweight as a BMI of 27 or higher.

The participants were divided into groups based on their menopausal status: premenopausal (before menopause), perimenopausal (during the menopause transition), and postmenopausal (after menopause).

Each group included between 142 and 225 females who either received orforglipron or placebo, an inactive pill with none of the drug in it.

The ATTAIN-1 study focused on people who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes. ATTAIN-2 included participants who had both overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The purpose of analyzing these two groups separately was to understand how orforglipron works in people with different health conditions.

The researchers measured several outcomes over a period of 72 weeks. They examined changes in body weight, waist circumference (the distance around the waist), and the waist-to-height ratio, a measure used to assess body fat distribution.

They also tracked how many women reached specific weight loss goals, such as losing at least 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% of their body weight, compared to those who took the inactive pill.

By studying these factors, the researchers were able to determine not only whether orforglipron helped women lose weight but also how much weight loss was achieved and how it affected their body shape.

The results showed that women who took orforglipron experienced significant weight loss regardless of their menopausal status.

In the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies, premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal women all lost an average of up to 14% of their body weight.

This means that the medication was effective for women at different life stages, including those experiencing menopause, when weight gain is often a challenge.

In addition to losing body weight, women in the orforglipron groups also saw meaningful reductions in waist circumference. Waist measurements decreased by up to 12.5 centimeters (about 5 inches) across all menopausal groups in both studies.

This reduction is important because greater visceral fat is associated with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

The waist-to-height ratio also improved for many women taking orforglipron. More participants treated with the medication moved into lower waist-to-height ratio categories than those who took the placebo.

This indicates a healthier distribution of body fat and suggests a lower risk of heart disease.

When looking at the number of women who reached specific weight loss milestones, orforglipron performed much better than the placebo. Up to 83% of women on orforglipron lost at least 5% of their body weight, while 30% of women on placebo reached that same level of weight loss.

Losing 5% or more of body weight is often considered clinically meaningful, as it can lead to improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.

Overall, these findings suggest that orforglipron is a promising new medication for weight management in women with obesity or overweight, including those who also have type 2 diabetes.

This can be especially helpful for those navigating the challenges of menopause while trying to manage their weight.

James J. Chao, MD, FACS, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of VedaNu Wellness, wasn’t involved in the research, but said the significance of these findings for postmenopausal women.

“The 14% is what’s grabbing headlines,” he told Healthline, “but up to 12.5 cm from the waistline is what I’m interested in.”

According to Chao, as females enter postmenopause, they tend to store more fat around their midsection.

“This is the type of fat that can cause heart disease,” he said. “So a pill that can help a 38-year-old woman lose the same amount as a 62-year-old breaks that myth.”

Additionally, in contrast to most GLP-1 drugs, which are injectable, it’s a once-a-day pill. You can also take it any time, Chao explained, making it more convenient.

“No needle, no refrigerator, and up to 83% of participants lost at least 5%,” he said. “Sometimes it’s the simple things that make a difference.”

Luca Moretti, MD, a medical doctor at Sapienza University of Rome, who wasn’t involved in the studies, added that convenience isn’t the only thing to consider when deciding whether to use orforglipron.

Obesity management should begin with an individualized plan that includes nutrition, physical activity, and the management of other risk factors.

“When these measures are not sufficient, adding pharmacological treatment can be considered together with a physician,” he told Healthline.

Moretti further advised speaking with your physician about any potential side effects, your existing medical conditions, other medications you are taking, and your treatment preferences.

“So the most useful question to ask a doctor is not simply, ‘Is Foundayo more convenient?’ but rather: ‘Among the available treatments, which one offers the best balance of effectiveness, tolerability, and practicality for me?'” he said.

#4838. An Easy 3 Miles with On’s Cloudsurfer 3

After years of stubborn loyalty to another brand, could one city jog make a longtime runner reconsider his shoes?

After just a mile in On's Cloudsurfer 3, it dawned on me—I’ve been far too hard-headed when it comes to my choice of running shoes.

For years, I held steadfastly to a particular brand and style, year after year, run after run. When one pair wore out, leaving my shins aching and feet tender, I’d quickly order a replacement online without even a thought of pivoting. Different colors and patterns kept it interesting, but that was the extent of my athletic audacity.

Truthfully, it wasn’t about brand loyalty. I wouldn’t dare try another shoe by the same company. It was more a case of preferring what I had grown used to in the past decade over the potential thrill of experimentation.

When I was asked to take On’s Cloudsurfer 3 for a jaunt, I was skeptical. Not that the shoes couldn’t or wouldn’t be great—it’s On, after all, a company renowned for exceptional technology and an ultralightweight feel to their sneaks—but that they’d be able to win over someone like me.

Still, I was game. The assignment called for my honest opinion during a three-mile run, and I was ready to break out of my rut (or at least try to). So I laced up and headed out on a beautiful early-fall Sunday afternoon in New York City. Here’s how it went.

I was intrigued even before I took my first step. Putting on Cloudsurfer 3, it immediately felt lighter than my go-to shoes. That surprised me, considering the minimal weight of my faves is what originally attracted me to them. The knit-mesh on the outside of the Cloudsurfer 3 was light and airy, and the inside was plush in all the right places (including the generous ankle collar) without being overbearing.

Yet, I knew the bigger test was to come. As a long-time sand volleyball player, I’ve developed a harder-than-necessary plant of my foot when I run, so I tend to need soft cushioning from a shoe.

Heading outside, I took a breath and set off down the sidewalk. The first strides were cautious, as I focused on the new sensation. The initial feedback was encouraging. It all felt effortless and soft, which I later would learn was due to On’s proprietary Surreal™ Superfoam with CloudTec®. I knew of On’s “run on clouds” tagline, but now I was feeling it in action, and I liked the smooth, soft ride I was experiencing.

I was a half-mile in when I hit my first red light—an unavoidable hazard of city running—giving me a moment to stop and reflect. “That was easier than usual,” I thought. I appreciated the secure feel of my ankle without it being too constricting, and my foot didn’t shift at all in the propulsive phase of my gait. The toe box was nice and comfy.

Pleasantly surprised so far, I changed my route on the fly and headed into Central Park. I wanted to test out the Cloudsurfer 3 on the oval around the Great Lawn . . . and enjoy an uninterrupted 0.55-mile loop.

I was breathing a little heavier at this point, but I noticed something about the shoe: It gave me the sensation of running downhill, even on a flat surface. I also felt what I’d call a “rebound” effect as each foot touched down and lifted off. This energy return made me feel faster than usual, with a burst of extra power on my “swing” phase and increased confidence in my mechanics. Could the Cloudsurfer 3’s mere 10.8 ounces per shoe be the difference maker?

I don’t know if it was the refreshing chill in the air, the clearer path than I’m used to in the city, or an extra “oomph” that the shoes’ softness provided, but I did a doubletake when seeing my 10:02 split time at the end of the second mile—well ahead of my typically slow 11-minute pace.

After two treks around the Great Lawn, I was back on the paved trail that leads out of the park. The sweat was beading despite a comfortable temperature in the high 60s, but I was enjoying the workout.

By the last mile, my legs were feeling good thanks to the easy two miles prior. I was in “go” mode and barely noticed my shoes. I decided to switch up my routine and finish with a series of sprints on the city blocks—fast bursts between intersections, with short rests at red lights.

Everything was still flowing smoothly: an effortless “lift” on each step, a seamless heel-to-toe transition, and no reverberations from the hard sidewalk and street underfoot. The last third of the run seemed to fly by, and I was more than happy with yet another sub-11-minute mile. I also realized that a fresh scrape on my ankle from a volleyball match earlier in the week, which I had been worried about aggravating during the run, was completely pain free; there was no chafing whatsoever.

When I took this assignment, I knew I’d likely be impressed with On’s Cloudsurfer 3. This is no ordinary sneaker, after all, but one designed with Swiss precision and an array of features celebrated by regular Joes and top-tier marathoners alike.

What I wasn’t quite ready for was the thought that maybe, just maybe, it was time to move on from my old standbys. I do know one thing as I reflect on the experience: My daily runs will be in On’s Cloudsurfer 3 because its soft, smooth ride made this run feel effortless.

#4837. The Ethical Dilemma of Therapists Who Don’t Work With Autistic People

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Recently, I attended a social gathering with a group of mental health providers. As people were talking, I heard someone make the comment, “Oh, I don’t work with autistic people.” I was not surprised by this comment, as I have heard many colleagues say similar things in a number of professional settings over the years. I was also not surprised to observe that most of the other therapists present either offered neutral responses or agreed that they too didn’t work with autistic people.

As an autistic provider and disability rights advocate, I knew I needed to take action. After this incident, I began including an exercise in a training I offer on the intersectionality of neurodevelopmental disabilities and mental health struggles. I have people write down a minority population, then ask them to fill in the following sentence with the group that they chose: “I don’t work with _____ people.”

While most mental health professionals have no objections to someone stating that they don’t work with autistic people, they become quite uncomfortable when they are asked to say, “I don’t work with Black people,” “I don’t work with gay people,” etc., because this statement suddenly feels like an ethics violation.

Someone excluding clients due to their race, ethnicity, gender, or other minority identity would not be tolerated by colleagues; the decision could even lead to serious professional consequences. If this is the case for other minorities, why does the profession look the other way when many providers routinely exclude clients based on their disabilities? One study by Cantor et al. (2020), for example, found that after calling more than 8000 mental health clinics across the US, only 47% would take a referral for a child with autism.

Over the course of history, neurodevelopmentally disabled people have been othered by society. Up until the last few decades, people with neurodevelopmental disabilities (ND) who had high support needs or could not mask fully were often put in institutions, hidden away from the rest of society. Gen X is the first generation whose disabled members have been allowed to live fully in their communities. Because of this, mental healthcare has all but ignored this population. There are few evidence-based mental health treatment modalities for autistic people or people with intellectual disabilities because researchers have only recently begun to study the topic in depth. There is also little instruction in mental health training programs about ND.

It’s no wonder that so many therapists feel unequipped to treat this community.

There is another reason why no one objected when that colleague stated that they don’t work with autistic people. This reason has to do with competency. The NASW Code of Ethics contains the following ethical principle, “Social workers practice within their areas of competence and develop and enhance their professional expertise.” If our mental health training programs are not ensuring that professionals are instructed on how to treat autistic and intellectually disabled clients with co-occurring mental health struggles, then it makes sense that they would feel that they were not competent to do so. If the therapist does not feel competent, they would avoid treating the client in order to avoid an ethical violation.

The problem with using competence to dismiss the responsibility of treating a minority population that tends to struggle with mental health at significantly higher rates than the general population is that it becomes a social justice concern that violates other ethical principles. Again, using The NASW Code of Ethics, this becomes a violation of the following ethical principles:

This ethical dilemma isn’t exclusive to social workers. The American Counseling Association Code of Ethics values professional competence, but also has principles that create a dilemma.

In my intersectionality training, after completing the exercise described above, I ask the following discussion question: “When is it responsible practice to refer a neurodivergent person to a specialist and when is it ableism?”

For those reading this post, I pose the same question.

Competence is important, and research has shown that ND clients do better when therapy is modified to meet their diverse learning needs. However, because the system does so little to train therapists to feel competent, it has created a mental health crisis. For example, autistic people are 9 times more likely to die by suicide than the general population. As a profession, we can no longer sit back and do nothing to meet the needs of ND clients because of a lack of competence. It’s time to learn about the mental health needs of ND people and address the competing principles in this ethical dilemma.

American Counseling Association. (2014). ACA code of ethics. counseling.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/ethics/2014-aca-code-of-ethics.pdf

Camm-Crosbie, L., Bradley, L., Shaw, R., Baron-Cohen, S., & Cassidy, S. (2019). “People like me don’t get support”: Autistic adults’ experiences of support and treatment for mental health difficulties, self-injury and suicidality. Autism: The International Journal of Research & Practice, 23(6), 1431–1441. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1362361318816053

Cantor, J., McBain, R. K., Kofner, A., Stein, B. D., & Hao Yu. (2020). Fewer than half of US mental health treatment facilities provide services for children with autism spectrum disorder. Health Affairs, 39(6), 968–974. https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2019.01557

Cork, J., (2025). What's your anxiety level? Cognitive behavioral therapy for neurodivergent children and teens with co-occurring anxiety disorders. Routledge Press.

National Association of Social Workers. (2021). Code of ethics of the National Association of Social Workers. National Association of Social Workers. socialworkers.org/About/Ethics/Code-of-Ethics/Code-of-Ethics-English

#4836. New Jersey may finally reverse its draconian e-bike law after massive backlash

New Jersey lawmakers are already looking to walk back one of the country’s most controversial e-bike laws, just months after the sweeping new regulations took effect and sparked widespread backlash from riders, bicycle shops, and advocacy groups.

A newly introduced bill, S4830, sponsored by State Senator Raj Mukherji, would remove licensing, registration, and insurance requirements for low-speed electric bicycles with motors rated at 750W or less and a maximum motor-powered speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). This includes Class 1 and Class 2 electric bicycles.

The proposal would essentially restore bicycle-like treatment for these two classes of e-bikes, importantly including throttle-equipped models that make up the majority of e-bikes sold in the state and more broadly in the US, while maintaining stricter requirements for faster and more powerful electric bicycles.

The move comes after New Jersey’s previous governor, Phil Murphy, signed a sweeping e-bike law in January following several tragic crashes involving young riders.

That legislation, which took full effect in July, eliminated the state’s previous three-class e-bike framework and introduced licensing and registration requirements for all electric bicycles, including ordinary low-speed commuter models. Throttle-equipped and faster e-bikes also faced insurance requirements.

As we previously reported, New Jersey bicycle shops experienced devastating sales declines after the law took effect, with some reporting drops of 20% to 90%. Several businesses were forced to lay off employees, downsize, or even close entirely as e-bike sales and usage plummeted.

Meanwhile, riders faced confusing new requirements that made e-bikes considerably less accessible, which was particularly impactful for lower-income residents, people with disabilities, and those who rely on electric bicycles for daily transportation.

I own a Class 3 e-bike, but I also acknowledge that with its potential assisted speed of 28mph it's of a different breed than Class 1/2 bikes -- that's just too fast in crowded bike lanes or shared use paths.

The first priority should be to target reckless riding by anyone, and illegal bikes should be confiscated if they're involved.

The original law was intended to improve safety, but critics argued that it largely punished responsible riders instead of addressing the growing problem of high-powered electric motorcycles masquerading as bicycles. Only responsible riders actually registered their bikes as required by law, while others were deterred from cycling, and the hooligan riders who often gave e-bikes a bad name continued to ride illegally.

After all, requiring someone riding a 20 mph (32 km/h) commuter e-bike to obtain a driver’s license and register their bicycle does little to address reckless riding on machines capable of highway speeds.

The newly proposed legislation appears to acknowledge that distinction, offering a more targeted approach that could preserve reasonable safety regulations without making ordinary e-bike ownership unnecessarily complicated.

S4830 still needs to work its way through the legislature before becoming law, but for New Jersey’s struggling e-bike industry, it’s a promising sign that lawmakers may finally be listening. It is still widely argued that requiring electric bicycles from 21-28 mph (32-45 km/h) to require a driver’s license and registration is overly burdensome, but at least the state appears to be moving back toward the right direction.
